Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Using $\text{CCl}_4$ instead of $\text{CHCl}_3$ introduces a trichloromethyl group ($-\text{CCl}_3$) onto the phenoxide ring, which on basic hydrolysis yields salicylic acid.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What is the intermediate formed on the benzene ring before the gem-dichloride hydrolyzes in the Reimer-Tiemann reaction?

options.text: Dichloromethyl phenoxide derivative ($-\text{CHCl}_2$ attached to the ortho position)

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Electrophilic attack by :\!\text{CCl}_2$ followed by proton transfer gives an ortho-dichloromethyl substituted intermediate ($o-\text{HO-C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{CHCl}_2$).

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: Why is the ortho-isomer (salicylaldehyde) the major product over the para-isomer in the Reimer-Tiemann reaction?

options.text: Because the para position is sterically hindered
Because para-salicylaldehyde is unstable and explodes
Due to coordination (chelation) of the $\text{Na}^+$ ion with the phenoxide oxygen and the attacking carbene, stabilizing the ortho transition state
Because ortho is the only position that has hydrogen

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Chelation by the metal counterion ($\text{Na}^+$) brings the electrophilic dichlorocarbene into close spatial proximity to the ortho position, favoring ortho-substitution.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: When pyrrole is treated with chloroform and strong alkali in the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, what abnormal ring-expanded product is obtained?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Abnormal Reimer-Tiemann reaction of pyrrole involves carbene addition across the $\text{C}=\text{C}$ bond to form a cyclopropane intermediate that undergoes ring expansion to 3-chloropyridine.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What is the hybridization and formal charge of the carbene carbon in singlet dichlorocarbene (:\!\text{CCl}_2)?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Singlet dichlorocarbene is neutral (formal charge 0) and $\text{sp}^2$ hybridized with a lone pair in one $\text{sp}^2$ orbital and an empty p orbital.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What happens when o-cresol (2-methylphenol) is subjected to the Reimer-Tiemann reaction with $\text{CHCl}_3 / \text{NaOH}$?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Formylation occurs at the vacant ortho position to give 2-hydroxy-3-methylbenzaldehyde, alongside cyclohexadienone side-products.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What is the abnormal (neutral cyclohexadienone) product obtained when p-cresol (4-methylphenol) undergoes Reimer-Tiemann reaction?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Attack of :\!\text{CCl}_2$ at the methyl-bearing para position forms a non-aromatic dienone that cannot rearomatize by losing a proton, isolating 4-methyl-4-(dichloromethyl)cyclohexa-2,5-dienone.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: Why is phenol much more reactive than benzene in the Reimer-Tiemann reaction?

options.text: Phenol is an acid and benzene is a base
Phenol is converted by $\text{NaOH}$ into phenoxide ion, which has high electron density on the aromatic ring via $+M$ effect

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Deprotonation creates phenoxide ($-\text{O}^-$), whose powerful $+M$ electron donation dramatically accelerates electrophilic aromatic substitution by the neutral carbene.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: How many moles of $\text{NaOH}$ are consumed overall per mole of phenol in the complete conversion to salicylaldehyde by the Reimer-Tiemann reaction?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: 1 mole deprotonates phenol, 1 mole generates carbene from $\text{CHCl}_3$, and 2 moles hydrolyze the gem-dichloride ($-\text{CHCl}_2 \rightarrow -\text{CHO}$). Total = 4 moles.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What is the intermediate formed when the gem-dichloride ($-\text{CHCl}_2$) is hydrolyzed by aqueous $\text{NaOH}$?

options.text: An unstable gem-diol ($-\text{CH(OH)}_2$), which spontaneously loses water to form an aldehyde ($-\text{CHO}$)

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Nucleophilic substitution of two chlorines by hydroxide forms a geminal diol, which immediately loses water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$) to give the aldehyde.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds gives a positive Reimer-Tiemann reaction to yield a formylated product?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Electron-rich aromatic systems such as phenols, naphthols, and certain heteroaromatics (pyrrole, indole) react smoothly under Reimer-Tiemann conditions.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What is the product when $\beta$-naphthol (2-naphthol) undergoes Reimer-Tiemann reaction?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Formylation occurs selectively at the highly nucleophilic 1-position of 2-naphthol, yielding 1-formyl-2-naphthol.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: Why is salicylaldehyde easily separated from 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde by steam distillation?

options.text: Salicylaldehyde has intramolecular hydrogen bonding, making it steam-volatile, whereas 4-hydroxybenzaldehyde has intermolecular hydrogen bonding and is non-volatile
Salicylaldehyde is a gas at room temperature

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Intramolecular chelation in salicylaldehyde lowers its boiling point and prevents hydration, rendering it steam-volatile.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: In the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, why is the reaction carried out at moderate temperature ($60-70^\circ\text{C}$) rather than boiling?

options.text: Because carbene freezes at high temperatures
To prevent rapid volatilization and loss of chloroform ($b.p. \approx 61^\circ\text{C}$) and avoid excessive resinous polymer formation
Because water boils at $50^\circ\text{C}$ in alkali

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Chloroform boils at $61^\circ\text{C}$; vigorous boiling would vaporize the reagent out of the basic medium and promote tarring.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What is the role of acidification at the end of the Reimer-Tiemann reaction?

options.text: To oxidize the aldehyde to acid
To protonate sodium salicylaldehyde phenoxide and regenerate the free phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: The reaction medium is basic, so salicylaldehyde exists as the water-soluble sodium phenoxide salt; acidification precipitates/releases free salicylaldehyde.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What is the IUPAC name of salicylaldehyde?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Salicylaldehyde is systematically named 2-hydroxybenzaldehyde.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: When indole is treated with $\text{CHCl}_3$ and $\text{KOH}$, what abnormal ring-expansion product is formed?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Similar to pyrrole, indole undergoes carbene addition across the pyrrole ring followed by ring enlargement to yield 3-chloroquinoline.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: Which of the following haloforms will react with phenol and alkali to form salicylaldehyde?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Both $\text{CHCl}_3$ and $\text{CHBr}_3$ undergo $\alpha$-elimination to form dihalocarbenes (:\!\text{CCl}_2 and :\!\text{CBr}_2), which hydrolyze to the same aldehyde group.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What is the formal valence shell electron count around the carbene carbon in dichlorocarbene (:\!\text{CCl}_2)?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Carbene carbon has 2 bonding pairs (with Cl) and 1 non-bonding lone pair, totaling 6 electrons (electron deficient, hence electrophilic).

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What compound is produced when guaiacol (2-methoxyphenol) undergoes Reimer-Tiemann reaction?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Formylation occurs at the position para to the activating $-\text{OH}$ group (ortho position is blocked by $-\text{OCH}_3$), synthesizing vanillin.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What happens to the optical activity of chiral compounds if a carbene undergoes insertion into a $\text{C-H}$ bond?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Singlet carbene insertions proceed via a concerted three-center transition state, retaining stereochemistry.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: Why is the yield of the Reimer-Tiemann reaction generally modest (typically $30-50\%$)?

options.text: Because phenol does not dissolve in water
Due to competing hydrolysis of chloroform by alkali, formation of unreactive tars, and abnormal non-aromatic dienone products
Because salicylaldehyde decomposes in air immediately
Because dichlorocarbene is an inert gas

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Direct attack of hydroxide on chloroform gives formate and carbon monoxide, consuming the reagent, alongside resinification.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: When 2,6-dimethylphenol is subjected to the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, what is the major aromatic product?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Since both ortho positions are blocked by methyl groups, formylation takes place exclusively at the vacant para position.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: In the mechanism of the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, what is the nature of the first bond formed between the phenoxide ring and dichlorocarbene?

options.text: An ionic bond between $\text{Cl}^-$ and oxygen
A covalent carbon-carbon bond formed by nucleophilic attack of the ortho carbon of phenoxide onto the empty p orbital of :\!\text{CCl}_2

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: The nucleophilic enolate-like ortho-carbon of phenoxide donates electrons to the empty orbital of neutral dichlorocarbene, creating a new $\text{C-C}$ bond.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What is the characteristic color given by salicylaldehyde with neutral ferric chloride ($\text{FeCl}_3$) solution?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Salicylaldehyde contains a free phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group that forms a colored coordination complex with $\text{Fe}^{3+}$ ions.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds will form a white crystalline bisulfite adduct?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Salicylaldehyde contains an accessible formyl carbonyl that readily adds sodium bisulfite to form a crystalline addition compound.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What happens when resorcinol (benzene-1,3-diol) undergoes Reimer-Tiemann reaction?

options.text: Formylation occurs between or ortho to the two hydroxyl groups yielding 2,4-dihydroxybenzaldehyde

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Resorcinol is intensely activated by two meta-hydroxyl groups and is readily formylated to 2,4-dihydroxybenzaldehyde.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: Why is $\text{KOH}$ sometimes used instead of $\text{NaOH}$ in the Reimer-Tiemann reaction?

options.text: $\text{KOH}$ changes the ortho/para ratio, sometimes increasing the proportion of the para isomer due to different cation chelation strength

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: The larger $\text{K}^+$ cation chelates less strongly with phenoxide oxygen and the incoming carbene, allowing more substitution at the para position.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: Identify the gas formed by the side reaction of chloroform with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$:
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Hydrolysis of dichlorocarbene in alkaline solution produces carbon monoxide: $:\!\text{CCl}_2 + 2\text{OH}^- \rightarrow \text{CO} + 2\text{Cl}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What is the product of the reaction: $\text{Phenol} + \text{CCl}_4 + \text{NaOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+} X$?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Using carbon tetrachloride ($\text{CCl}_4$) in the Reimer-Tiemann reaction gives salicylic acid as the major product.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What test can distinguish salicylaldehyde from salicylic acid?

options.text: Sodium bicarbonate test ($\text{NaHCO}_3$): salicylic acid evolves $\text{CO}_2$ effervescence, while salicylaldehyde does not

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Salicylic acid has a carboxylic acid group strong enough to decompose sodium bicarbonate and liberate $\text{CO}_2$; the weak phenolic acid of salicylaldehyde cannot.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What is the oxidation state of the formyl carbon in salicylaldehyde?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: The formyl carbon has bonds to C ($0$), H ($-1$), and O ($+2$), giving net oxidation state $+1$.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: During Reimer-Tiemann reaction of phenol, how is excess unreacted chloroform removed during work-up?

options.text: By fractional distillation or steam distillation before acidifying the reaction mixture

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Steam distillation of the alkaline mixture volatilizes and removes excess chloroform without distilling the non-volatile sodium phenoxide salts.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: Which of the following phenols gives ONLY an abnormal cyclohexadienone product upon Reimer-Tiemann reaction?

options.text: 2,4,6-Trimethylphenol (Mesitol - all reactive ortho and para positions are blocked by methyl groups)

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Mesitol has methyl groups at positions 2, 4, and 6; carbene attack at any of these positions leads to dearomatized cyclohexadienone structures with no proton to lose.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What is the rate-determining step in the formation of dichlorocarbene from chloroform?

options.text: Loss of chloride ion from the trichloromethanide anion ($:\!\text{CCl}_3^- \rightarrow :\!\text{CCl}_2 + \text{Cl}^-$)

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Deprotonation is fast and reversible; the slower $\alpha$-elimination of $\text{Cl}^-$ from $\text{CCl}_3^-$ determines the rate of carbene generation.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What type of intermediate species is generated when dichlorocarbene adds to the phenoxide ring?

options.text: A non-aromatic resonance-stabilized carbanionic cyclohexadienyl intermediate

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Electrophilic attack generates a pentadienyl-type anion carrying negative charge distributed over oxygen and the ring, which rearomatizes by proton loss.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: Why is phase-transfer catalysis (PTC) often utilized in modern Reimer-Tiemann procedures?

options.text: To transfer hydroxide ions from the aqueous layer into the organic chloroform layer, drastically improving carbene generation and aldehyde yields
To remove the smell of phenol

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: PTC catalysts (like quaternary ammonium salts) transport ions across the organic-aqueous phase boundary, speeding up carbene formation.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: When thymol (2-isopropyl-5-methylphenol) is subjected to the Reimer-Tiemann reaction, formylation occurs at:

options.text: The vacant position ortho to $-\text{OH}$ and para to isopropyl

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Formylation occurs predominantly at the open position 4 (para to isopropyl and ortho to hydroxyl).

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: Identify the compound that will NOT give a positive Tollens' test after undergoing the standard Reimer-Tiemann reaction with $\text{CHCl}_3$:

options.text: A compound that yields a ketone or carboxylic acid instead of an aldehyde

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Reactions yielding aldehydes (salicylaldehydes) give positive Tollens' tests, whereas products of $\text{CCl}_4$ (salicylic acid) do not.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What is the product when catechol (benzene-1,2-diol) undergoes Reimer-Tiemann reaction?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Formylation occurs on the activated ring, yielding isomeric dihydroxybenzaldehydes.

Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.question: What classic medicinal compound is commercially produced starting from salicylaldehyde via Perkin condensation?
Reimer-Tiemann Reaction.explanation: Salicylaldehyde undergoes Perkin condensation with acetic anhydride and sodium acetate to synthesize coumarin, the foundational scaffold for dicoumarol anticoagulants.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What are the primary reagents and conditions used in Kolbe's Reaction (Kolbe-Schmitt Reaction)?

options.text: Sodium phenoxide heated with carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$) at $400\text{ K}$ and $4-7\text{ atm}$ pressure, followed by acidification
Phenol with carbon monoxide at room temperature
Phenol with formic acid and sulfuric acid
Sodium phenoxide with chloroform and sodium hydroxide

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Kolbe's reaction involves heating sodium phenoxide with dry $\text{CO}_2$ gas under pressure ($4-7\text{ atm}$) at $120-140^\circ\text{C}$ ($400\text{ K}$), followed by acid hydrolysis to produce salicylic acid.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the major organic product obtained from Kolbe's reaction using sodium phenoxide?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Sodium phenoxide selectively carboxylates at the ortho position to yield sodium salicylate, which upon acidification gives salicylic acid (2-hydroxybenzoic acid).

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the electrophile in Kolbe's reaction?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Carbon dioxide ($\text{O}=\text{C}=\text{O}$) is a neutral, relatively weak electrophile whose electrophilicity stems from the electron-deficient central carbon atom.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: Why is sodium phenoxide used instead of phenol itself in Kolbe's reaction?

options.text: Phenol decomposes upon heating with carbon dioxide
Phenol is a gas at $400\text{ K}$
Phenol does not dissolve in water
Phenoxide ion is vastly more nucleophilic than neutral phenol, making the aromatic ring sufficiently electron-rich to attack the weak electrophile $\text{CO}_2$

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: $\text{CO}_2$ is a weak electrophile and cannot attack neutral phenol; the phenoxide ion ($-\text{O}^-$) strongly activates the aromatic ring via $+M$ electron donation.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What happens to the product distribution if potassium phenoxide is used instead of sodium phenoxide at higher temperatures ($>200^\circ\text{C}$)?

options.text: Salicylic acid is still the only product

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: The larger $\text{K}^+$ ion coordinates less tightly than $\text{Na}^+$; at elevated temperatures, thermodynamic control shifts carboxylation preferentially to the less hindered para position, yielding 4-hydroxybenzoic acid.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: Why does sodium phenoxide favor carboxylation at the ortho position (giving salicylic acid)?

options.text: Because the para position has no hydrogen atoms
Due to the formation of a stable, chelated 6-membered cyclic transition state involving the $\text{Na}^+$ cation, phenoxide oxygen, and $\text{CO}_2$
Because ortho is always less crowded than para

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: The small $\text{Na}^+$ cation coordinates simultaneously to the phenoxide oxygen and a $\text{CO}_2$ oxygen, creating a six-membered chelate ring that delivers $\text{CO}_2$ directly to the ortho carbon.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What critical pharmaceutical medicine is commercially synthesized by acetylating salicylic acid obtained from Kolbe's reaction?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Salicylic acid reacts with acetic anhydride in the presence of an acid catalyst to produce acetylsalicylic acid, universally known as Aspirin.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the chemical reaction for the synthesis of aspirin from salicylic acid?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Acetylation of the phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group of salicylic acid by acetic anhydride produces acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin) and acetic acid as a byproduct.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the commercial product called 'Oil of Wintergreen', prepared from salicylic acid?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Esterification of salicylic acid with methanol in the presence of concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ gives methyl salicylate, known as Oil of Wintergreen.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is 'Salol', and how is it synthesized from salicylic acid?

options.text: Methyl salicylate, used as a pain balm
Phenyl salicylate, used as an intestinal antiseptic; prepared by heating salicylic acid with phenol in the presence of $\text{POCl}_3$
Sodium salicylate, used as table salt
Acetyl salicylate, used as an antibiotic

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Phenyl salicylate (Salol) is synthesized by reacting salicylic acid with phenol in the presence of $\text{POCl}_3$; it acts as an intestinal antiseptic because it does not hydrolyze in the acidic stomach.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: Why must the sodium phenoxide used in the Kolbe-Schmitt reaction be completely anhydrous?

options.text: Because water causes an explosion with $\text{CO}_2$
Because water evaporates and raises the pressure too high
Because water reacts with carbon dioxide to form carbonic acid, neutralizing the phenoxide to phenol and halting the reaction
Because water converts salicylic acid into benzene

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Moisture converts phenoxide back to neutral phenol, which is unreactive toward $\text{CO}_2$, drastically lowering or completely destroying the reaction yield.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the physical state and structure of carbon dioxide ($\text{CO}_2$)?

options.text: Linear molecule with zero dipole moment, $\text{O}=\text{C}=\text{O}$, $\text{sp}$ hybridized central carbon

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: $\text{CO}_2$ is linear with $\text{sp}$ hybridized carbon; the two electronegative oxygen atoms pull electron density away, making the central carbon electrophilic.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the oxidation state of the carboxyl carbon in salicylic acid?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: The carbon is bonded to one aromatic carbon ($0$), one single-bonded oxygen ($+1$), and double-bonded oxygen ($+2$), giving net oxidation state $+3$.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What gas is evolved when salicylic acid is treated with aqueous sodium bicarbonate ($\text{NaHCO}_3$)?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: The $-\text{COOH}$ group of salicylic acid is more acidic than carbonic acid ($pK_a \approx 2.97$ vs $6.35$), so it liberates brisk effervescence of $\text{CO}_2$ gas.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: Why is salicylic acid significantly more acidic than benzoic acid ($pK_a = 2.97$ vs $4.20$)?

options.text: Because the $-\text{OH}$ group is electron-withdrawing via resonance
Because salicylic acid is an inorganic acid
Due to strong intramolecular hydrogen bonding between the phenolic $-\text{OH}$ and the carboxylate oxygen (ortho effect / chelation of conjugate base)
Because benzoic acid cannot form hydrogen bonds with water

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: The salicylate monoanion is exceptionally stabilized by an intramolecular hydrogen bond: the phenolic $-\text{OH}$ proton chelates to the negative carboxylate oxygen, drastically increasing acidity.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What color appears when salicylic acid is mixed with neutral $\text{FeCl}_3$ solution?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: The phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group forms an intense violet-colored iron(III) salicylate chelate complex.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What happens when salicylic acid is heated with soda lime ($\text{NaOH} + \text{CaO}$)?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Soda lime heating decarboxylates the $-\text{COOH}$ group of salicylic acid, liberating $\text{Na}_2\text{CO}_3$ and leaving phenol.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What happens when salicylic acid is heated with zinc dust?

options.text: Reduction of the phenolic group occurs to yield Benzoic acid

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Zinc dust specifically reduces the phenolic hydroxyl group of salicylic acid to a $\text{C-H}$ bond, yielding benzoic acid.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the product when sodium 2-naphtholate is subjected to Kolbe's reaction at $120-140^\circ\text{C}$?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: At moderate temperatures ($120-140^\circ\text{C}$), carboxylation of 2-naphthol occurs kinetically at the 1-position to yield 2-hydroxy-1-naphthoic acid.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What happens when sodium 2-naphtholate is heated with $\text{CO}_2$ at elevated temperatures ($200-250^\circ\text{C}$, BON acid synthesis)?

options.text: Carboxylation occurs at the thermodynamically stable 3-position, yielding 3-hydroxy-2-naphthoic acid (BON acid)

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: At higher temperatures, the reaction is reversible and thermodynamic control yields 3-hydroxy-2-naphthoic acid (Beta-Oxy-Naphthoic or BON acid, an important azo dye intermediate).

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the effect of having electron-donating substituents (like $-\text{OCH}_3$ or $-\text{CH}_3$) on the phenoxide ring during Kolbe's reaction?

options.text: They further increase ring electron density, facilitating carboxylation even under atmospheric pressure or milder conditions
They cause the phenoxide to decompose into methane

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Strong electron donors like additional $-\text{OH}$ groups (e.g. resorcinol) allow carboxylation simply by bubbling $\text{CO}_2$ through an aqueous bicarbonate solution.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: Why does resorcinol (1,3-dihydroxybenzene) carboxylate under much milder conditions than phenol in Kolbe's reaction?

options.text: The two mutually meta-hydroxyl groups reinforce ring nucleophilicity, enabling carboxylation with aqueous $\text{KHCO}_3$ at $100^\circ\text{C}$

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: The two $-\text{OH}$ groups synergistically enhance electron density at the 4-position, giving 2,4-dihydroxybenzoic acid without needing high pressure.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the IUPAC name of salicylic acid?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: The IUPAC name of salicylic acid is 2-hydroxybenzoic acid.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the role of pressure ($4-7\text{ atm}$) in the industrial Kolbe-Schmitt synthesis of salicylic acid?

options.text: To keep the sodium phenoxide from freezing
To prevent the formation of aspirin
To increase the concentration and effective collision frequency of gaseous $\text{CO}_2$ at the solid/molten phenoxide surface

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Higher pressure dramatically enhances the solubility and surface contact of $\text{CO}_2$ with the phenoxide reactant, driving the equilibrium toward the salicylate salt.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the product obtained when salicylic acid is treated with bromine water in excess?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Excess bromine water causes bromination with simultaneous electrophilic ipso-decarboxylation of the $-\text{COOH}$ group, yielding 2,4,6-tribromophenol as a white precipitate.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What happens when salicylic acid is treated with concentrated nitric acid in the presence of concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$?

options.text: Picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol) is formed via nitration with ipso-decarboxylation

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Vigorous nitration introduces nitro groups with accompanying loss of the carboxyl group, giving picric acid (2,4,6-trinitrophenol).

Kolbe's Reaction.question: In the Kolbe reaction, what is the initial salt formed before acidification?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Carboxylation of sodium phenoxide by $\text{CO}_2$ produces sodium salicylate: $o-\text{HO-C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{COONa}$.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds does NOT give brisk effervescence with aqueous $\text{NaHCO}_3$?

options.text: Phenol ($pK_a \approx 10$, too weakly acidic to decompose bicarbonate)

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Phenol is a very weak acid ($pK_a \approx 10$) and does not react with sodium bicarbonate; carboxylic acids ($pK_a \approx 3-5$) react briskly to liberate $\text{CO}_2$.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the mechanism of the Kolbe-Schmitt reaction classified as?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: The reaction is an electrophilic aromatic substitution where the electron-rich phenoxide ring acts as the nucleophile and neutral $\text{CO}_2$ acts as the electrophile.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the role of the proton transfer step in the Kolbe-Schmitt mechanism after $\text{CO}_2$ attacks the phenoxide ortho carbon?

options.text: To restore aromaticity of the benzene ring by shifting the ring proton to the phenoxide oxygen / carboxylate group

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Electrophilic addition creates a non-aromatic cyclohexadienone intermediate; rapid proton loss restores aromatic resonance stabilization.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: Why is Aspirin (acetylsalicylic acid) preferred over pure salicylic acid for clinical use as an analgesic and antipyretic?

options.text: Salicylic acid has no medicinal effect
Salicylic acid causes severe irritation and bleeding of the stomach mucous lining, whereas acetylating the phenolic $-\text{OH}$ significantly reduces gastric irritation
Salicylic acid cannot dissolve in water

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Free salicylic acid is a harsh irritant to the gastric mucosa; masking the phenolic group as an acetate ester minimizes ulcerogenic side effects.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: When salicylic acid is treated with excess methanol and concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, which functional group undergoes esterification?

options.text: Both the $-\text{COOH}$ and $-\text{OH}$ groups form esters
The carboxylic acid group ($-\text{COOH}$) selectively forms an ester ($-\text{COOCH}_3$)

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Under Fischer esterification conditions, the carboxylic acid reacts with alcohol to form methyl salicylate; phenols do not readily form ethers or esters with alcohols in acid.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: When salicylic acid is treated with acetic anhydride, which functional group reacts?

options.text: The phenolic hydroxyl group ($-\text{OH}$) is acetylated to form an ester ($-\text{OCOCH}_3$)

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Acetic anhydride selectively acetylates the phenolic $-\text{OH}$ group to give acetylsalicylic acid (aspirin).

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the product when o-cresol (2-methylphenol) undergoes Kolbe's reaction?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Carboxylation occurs at the remaining open ortho position (position 6 relative to $-\text{OH}$), giving 3-methylsalicylic acid.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the product when p-cresol (4-methylphenol) undergoes Kolbe's reaction?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: The para position is occupied, so carboxylation takes place at one of the open ortho positions, yielding 5-methylsalicylic acid.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the molecular weight of Aspirin ($\text{C}_9\text{H}_8\text{O}_4$)?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: $\text{C}_9\text{H}_8\text{O}_4$: $(9\times 12) + (8\times 1) + (4\times 16) = 108 + 8 + 64 = 180\text{ g/mol}$.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds gives a negative ferric chloride ($\text{FeCl}_3$) test?

options.text: Aspirin (the phenolic $-\text{OH}$ is masked by an acetyl group)

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: In pure aspirin, the phenolic $-\text{OH}$ is acetylated to an ester, so it does NOT form the violet complex with $\text{FeCl}_3$ (unless hydrolyzed).

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What happens during the alkaline hydrolysis of aspirin inside the human body?

options.text: It is oxidized to carbon dioxide
It is hydrolyzed by esterases in the intestine and blood to salicylic acid and acetic acid
It decomposes into benzene and methane

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Aspirin acts as a prodrug: esterases cleave the acetyl ester to liberate active salicylic acid, which inhibits cyclooxygenase (COX) enzymes.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: Why is Kolbe's reaction often carried out in autoclave reactors on an industrial scale?

options.text: To cool the mixture below zero
To withstand and maintain the high $\text{CO}_2$ gas pressures ($5-10\text{ atm}$) and temperatures required for maximum yield

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Industrial Kolbe-Schmitt synthesis utilizes sealed, heated, pressurized steel autoclaves to achieve rapid conversion of dry sodium phenoxide.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the role of sulfuric acid in the acidification step of Kolbe's reaction?

options.text: To act as a dehydration agent
To protonate the carboxylate salt to precipitate free salicylic acid ($2\text{Ar-COONa} + \text{H}_2\text{SO}_4 \rightarrow 2\text{Ar-COOH} + \text{Na}_2\text{SO}_4$)

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Acidification converts the soluble sodium salicylate salt into free, sparingly water-soluble salicylic acid, which crystallizes out.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: Which of the following describes the difference between Kolbe's reaction and Reimer-Tiemann reaction?

options.text: Kolbe's introduces a carboxyl group ($-\text{COOH}$) using $\text{CO}_2$, whereas Reimer-Tiemann introduces a formyl group ($-\text{CHO}$) using $\text{CHCl}_3$
Kolbe's reaction reduces phenol, Reimer-Tiemann oxidizes it
Kolbe's produces an amine, Reimer-Tiemann produces an ether
Kolbe's works on benzene, Reimer-Tiemann works on methane

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Kolbe's reaction is a carboxylation producing salicylic acid; Reimer-Tiemann is a formylation producing salicylaldehyde.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: When salicylic acid is treated with phthalic anhydride in the presence of concentrated $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$, what occurs?

options.text: Esterification / condensation without forming phenolphthalein (since $-\text{OH}$ ortho position is blocked by $-\text{COOH}$)

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Phthalic anhydride requires unhindered para/ortho positions to form indicator phthaleins; salicylic acid behaves differently due to the carboxyl substituent.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: Identify the compound formed when salicylic acid is heated alone above $200^\circ\text{C}$:

options.text: Phenol, Carbon dioxide, and Phenyl salicylate (Salol by self-esterification)

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Thermal decomposition of salicylic acid causes decarboxylation to phenol and $\text{CO}_2$, and self-condensation between salicylic acid and generated phenol yields Salol.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: What is the primary commercial use of 3-hydroxy-2-naphthoic acid (BON acid) prepared by Kolbe's reaction?

options.text: Coupling component for Naphthol AS series azo dyes and pigments

Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: BON acid is the crucial intermediate for Naphthol AS, the foundation of azo dyes for textiles, plastics, and inks.

Kolbe's Reaction.question: Consider the sequence: $\text{Phenol} \xrightarrow{\text{NaOH}} A \xrightarrow{\text{CO}_2, 400\text{ K}, 4-7\text{ atm}} B \xrightarrow{\text{H}^+} C \xrightarrow{(\text{CH}_3\text{CO})_2\text{O} / \text{H}^+} D$. What is compound $D$?
Kolbe's Reaction.explanation: Phenol gives sodium phenoxide ($A$), then sodium salicylate ($B$), which on acidifying yields salicylic acid ($C$). Acetylation of $C$ yields Aspirin ($D$).

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What are the standard reactants in the Williamson Ether Synthesis?

options.text: An alkyl halide (or alkyl sulfonate) and an alkoxide (or phenoxide) ion
Two molecules of alcohol with concentrated sulfuric acid at $413\text{ K}$
An alkene and water in acid

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Williamson ether synthesis involves the bimolecular nucleophilic substitution ($S_N2$) of an alkyl halide with a sodium or potassium alkoxide or phenoxide.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the mechanism of the Williamson Ether Synthesis?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: The alkoxide ion acts as a nucleophile, attacking the backside of the primary alkyl halide with simultaneous expulsion of the halide leaving group in a single concerted $S_N2$ step.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: Which type of alkyl halide gives the best yield in Williamson Ether Synthesis?

options.text: Primary ($1^\circ$) alkyl halide or methyl halide

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Because alkoxide ions are strong bases, primary and methyl halides undergo smooth $S_N2$ displacement without competing $E2$ elimination.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What happens when a tertiary alkyl halide (e.g., tert-butyl bromide) is reacted with sodium ethoxide?

options.text: Substitution occurs to yield tert-butyl ethyl ether
An alcohol and an alkane are formed
Elimination ($E2$) predominates to yield an alkene (2-methylpropene) as the major product

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Alkoxides are strong bases; with sterically hindered $3^\circ$ halides, steric hindrance prevents backside $S_N2$ attack, making $E2$ elimination the exclusive pathway.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the best synthetic combination to prepare tert-butyl ethyl ether via Williamson synthesis?

options.text: Isobutylene and ethyl alcohol with base

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Using a primary alkyl halide ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$) with a hindered alkoxide allows $S_N2$ attack on the unhindered primary carbon to yield the ether cleanly.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: Can anisole (methoxybenzene) be prepared by reacting bromobenzene with sodium methoxide under Williamson conditions?

options.text: Yes, it gives a $100\%$ yield easily
No, because bromobenzene has partial double-bond character due to resonance and does not undergo $S_N2$ displacement
Yes, but only in the presence of water
No, because sodium methoxide is acidic

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Aryl halides are extremely unreactive toward nucleophilic substitution ($S_N2$) due to resonance stabilization of the $\text{C-X}$ bond and steric hindrance of the aromatic ring.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the correct combination of reagents to prepare anisole ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OCH}_3$) via Williamson synthesis?

options.text: Sodium phenoxide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$) and Methyl iodide ($\text{CH}_3\text{I}$) or dimethyl sulfate

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Phenoxide acts as a good nucleophile, attacking the unhindered methyl carbon of methyl iodide via $S_N2$ to form anisole in high yield.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the major product when sodium ethoxide reacts with 2-bromopropane?

options.text: Propene (predominant via $E2$ elimination) along with a minor amount of ethyl isopropyl ether

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Secondary alkyl halides react with strong bases like ethoxide to give predominantly elimination ($E2$) over substitution ($S_N2$).

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: Why is anhydrous condition strictly required in the Williamson Ether Synthesis?

options.text: Water hydrolyzes the alkoxide ion back to the parent alcohol and hydroxide: $R-\text{O}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightleftharpoons R-\text{OH} + \text{OH}^-$
Water oxidizes alkyl halides into carboxylic acids
Water causes ether to explode immediately

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Hydroxide formed by hydrolysis competes with alkoxide, attacking the alkyl halide to produce alcohols instead of ethers.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What base is typically used to prepare alkoxides from alcohols for Williamson synthesis?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Sodium hydride ($\text{NaH}$) or sodium metal irreversibly deprotonates alcohols ($R\text{OH} + \text{NaH} \rightarrow R\text{ONa} + \text{H}_2\uparrow$), producing strong, dry alkoxide nucleophiles.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the order of reactivity of alkyl halides in Williamson Ether Synthesis?

options.text: All halides react at the exact same rate

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Because the mechanism is strictly $S_N2$, reactivity is governed by steric accessibility to backside attack: methyl is fastest, tertiary gives $E2$ exclusively.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the order of leaving group ability of halides in Williamson synthesis?

options.text: Halides cannot act as leaving groups

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Iodide is the largest and weakest conjugate base, making it the best leaving group: alkyl iodides react fastest.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: Which of the following ethers CANNOT be synthesized by Williamson Ether Synthesis?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Diphenyl ether requires an aryl halide to react with a phenoxide ion; aryl halides do not undergo $S_N2$ displacement, so diphenyl ether cannot be prepared this way.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the stereochemical outcome at the chiral carbon of an alkyl halide undergoing Williamson Ether Synthesis?

options.text: Destruction of optical activity by free radicals

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Concerted backside nucleophilic attack in the $S_N2$ mechanism causes inversion of stereochemistry at the reacting electrophilic carbon center.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the product when $(R)$-2-bromobutane is treated with sodium methoxide?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: The substitution product undergoes complete inversion of configuration from $(R)$ to $(S)$.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the product when sodium phenoxide is treated with ethyl bromide?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^- + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OCH}_2\text{CH}_3 + \text{Br}^-$, synthesizing phenetole.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: Can di-tert-butyl ether be prepared by Williamson Ether Synthesis?

options.text: No, because reaction of tert-butoxide with tert-butyl halide yields 2-methylpropene exclusively via $E2$ elimination
Yes, by heating under high pressure

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Di-tert-butyl ether cannot be made by Williamson synthesis because any attempt pairs a bulky base with a tertiary halide, producing isobutylene via $E2$.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the product when 1-bromobutane is treated with sodium ethoxide?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Primary alkyl halide reacts with ethoxide via $S_N2$ to yield butyl ethyl ether cleanly.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: Why is dimethyl sulfate ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{SO}_4$) frequently used instead of methyl iodide in Williamson synthesis?

options.text: Because dimethyl sulfate is a gas
It is an inexpensive and highly effective methylating agent where the methyl sulfate anion is an excellent leaving group
Because methyl iodide does not react with alkoxides

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Dimethyl sulfate provides a reactive, unhindered methyl group with a stable methylsulfate leaving group, commonly used industrially for ether synthesis.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the intramolecular version of Williamson Ether Synthesis used to prepare?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Treating a halo-alcohol (halohydrin) with base forms an internal alkoxide that displaces the halide intramolecularly to form cyclic ethers (oxiranes/epoxides).

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: When 2-chloroethanol is treated with aqueous sodium hydroxide, what product is formed via intramolecular Williamson synthesis?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Base deprotonates the hydroxyl group to form $^-\text{OCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}$, which undergoes rapid intramolecular backside displacement to form the 3-membered ring oxirane.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: Why does intramolecular Williamson cyclization to form 3-membered epoxides occur rapidly despite ring strain?

options.text: Because 3-membered rings have no ring strain
Due to high effective local concentration and favorable proximity (entropy) of the alkoxide to the adjacent carbon bearing the leaving group
Because halogen bonds pull the atoms together

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: The intramolecular distance is extremely small, giving a high frequency of collision that overcomes unfavorable enthalpic ring strain.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the product of the reaction: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{ONa} \rightarrow$?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Benzyl chloride is a highly reactive primary benzylic halide that undergoes smooth $S_N2$ substitution with sodium ethoxide to yield benzyl ethyl ether.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: Why are crown ethers often added to Williamson Ether Synthesis mixtures?

options.text: To act as the alkylating agent
Crown ethers complex the alkali metal cation (e.g., 18-crown-6 for $\text{K}^+$), freeing the 'naked' alkoxide anion to dramatically enhance its nucleophilicity

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Sequestering the metal counterion separates ion pairs, increasing the energy and nucleophilic reactivity of the alkoxide anion.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What happens when neopentyl bromide ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{CCH}_2\text{Br}$) is treated with sodium ethoxide?

options.text: The reaction is extremely sluggish or fails because severe steric hindrance from the $\beta$-tert-butyl group blocks backside attack
It rapidly forms neopentyl ethyl ether via $S_N2$
It undergoes rapid $E2$ elimination to an alkene

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Neopentyl halides are primary but extremely sterically hindered by three methyl groups on the $\beta$-carbon, making $S_N2$ backside attack virtually impossible.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the product when sodium methoxide reacts with allyl bromide ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2\text{Br}$)?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Allyl bromide is exceptionally reactive toward $S_N2$ displacement due to allylic resonance stabilization of the transition state, giving allyl methyl ether rapidly.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the role of dipolar aprotic solvents (such as DMF, DMSO, or acetone) in Williamson Ether Synthesis?

options.text: They solvate the metal cation strongly while leaving the alkoxide anion poorly solvated and highly nucleophilic, speeding up $S_N2$

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Aprotic solvents do not form hydrogen bonds with anions, maximizing the nucleophilicity of alkoxides and boosting $S_N2$ rates by orders of magnitude.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: In the preparation of di-n-propyl ether, what are the reactants for Williamson synthesis?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Matching a 3-carbon alkoxide with a 3-carbon primary alkyl halide yields symmetrical di-n-propyl ether via $S_N2$.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: Which of the following pairs of reagents will successfully synthesize isopropyl methyl ether?

options.text: Isopropyl alcohol and methanol with concentrated $\text{HCl}$

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Pairing the bulky isopropoxide nucleophile with unhindered methyl iodide eliminates the possibility of $E2$ elimination, yielding isopropyl methyl ether cleanly.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the product when 4-chlorobutane-1-ol is treated with sodium hydride ($\text{NaH}$)?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Deprotonation of the hydroxyl group yields an alkoxide that attacks the terminal 4-carbon bearing chlorine, forming stable 5-membered cyclic ether tetrahydrofuran (THF).

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: Why is Williamson synthesis generally preferred over acid-catalyzed bimolecular dehydration of alcohols for preparing unsymmetrical ethers ($R-\text{O}-R'$)?

options.text: Williamson synthesis does not use chemicals

Acid-catalyzed dehydration of two different alcohols produces an inseparable mixture of three ethers ($R-\text{O}-R$, $R'-\text{O}-R'$, and $R-\text{O}-R'$), whereas Williamson synthesis gives a single ether selectively

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Mixing two different alcohols under acidic dehydration conditions yields symmetrical and unsymmetrical ethers indiscriminately, destroying selectivity.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the major organic product when sodium phenoxide is heated with methyl iodide?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Nucleophilic displacement of iodide by the oxygen of phenoxide yields anisole.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: When an alkyl halide is treated with silver oxide ($\text{Ag}_2\text{O}$, dry), what type of ether is formed?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Dry silver oxide acts as a mild source of oxide ion, reacting with two molecules of primary alkyl halide to produce symmetrical dialkyl ethers.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the product when sodium tert-butoxide reacts with methyl iodide?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Methyl iodide has no $\beta$-hydrogens and cannot undergo elimination; it undergoes fast $S_N2$ substitution with tert-butoxide to yield MTBE.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the commercial fuel additive MTBE, and how is it named systematically?

options.text: Methyl tert-butyl ether (2-Methoxy-2-methylpropane), an octane booster

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: MTBE is 2-methoxy-2-methylpropane, synthesized to replace tetraethyl lead as an anti-knock gasoline additive.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What happens when sodium ethoxide is treated with chlorobenzene at room temperature?

options.text: No reaction occurs due to the inertness of aryl halides toward $S_N2$

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Chlorobenzene does not undergo $S_N2$ displacement with alkoxides at room temperature because of ring aromaticity and partial double bond character.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: Under what extreme conditions can aryl halides react with alkoxides to form alkyl aryl ethers?

options.text: In the presence of strong electron-withdrawing groups (such as $-\text{NO}_2$) at ortho and para positions via the $S_N\text{Ar}$ (addition-elimination) mechanism

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Activated aryl halides (e.g., 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene) react with alkoxides via $S_N\text{Ar}$ Meisenheimer complexes, bypassing $S_N2$ restrictions.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: When 2,4-dinitrochlorobenzene is treated with sodium methoxide, the reaction is classified as:
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: The nitro groups stabilize the Meisenheimer anionic intermediate, enabling addition-elimination ($S_N\text{Ar}$).

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What happens when an alkyl sulfonate (like alkyl tosylate, $R-\text{OTs}$) is used instead of an alkyl halide in Williamson synthesis?

options.text: The reaction proceeds smoothly via $S_N2$ because tosylate is an excellent leaving group
The sulfonate group oxidizes the alkoxide

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Alkyl tosylates ($R-\text{OTs}$) and mesylates ($R-\text{OMs}$) possess exceptionally stable sulfonate leaving groups and undergo facile $S_N2$ displacement by alkoxides.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the product when $(S)$-butan-2-ol is converted to its tosylate and then reacted with sodium methoxide?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Tosylate formation retains stereochemistry at the chiral center; subsequent $S_N2$ displacement by methoxide inverts the configuration to $(R)$.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the product of: $\text{CH}_2=\text{CH}-\text{CH}_2-\text{ONa} + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{I} \rightarrow$?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Allyloxide displaces iodide from ethyl iodide via $S_N2$ to produce allyl ethyl ether.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: Why does reaction of sodium ethoxide with bromocyclohexane give predominantly cyclohexene?

options.text: Bromocyclohexane is a secondary halide and undergoes $E2$ elimination readily with the strong base ethoxide

Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Secondary halides undergo facile anti-periplanar $E2$ elimination with strong bases, giving the cycloalkene as the major product.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: Identify reagent $X$ in: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \xrightarrow{X} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{O}^-\text{Na}^+$:
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Alcohols are weaker acids than water, so strong bases like $\text{Na}$ metal or $\text{NaH}$ are needed for complete conversion to alkoxide.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: What is the product of intramolecular displacement in 5-bromopentan-1-ol with base?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Deprotonation of the terminal hydroxyl group generates an alkoxide that attacks C-5, expelling bromide to close a stable 6-membered tetrahydropyran ring.

Williamson Ether Synthesis.question: Which of the following ethers CANNOT be synthesized by Williamson method?
Williamson Ether Synthesis.explanation: Di-tert-butyl ether requires reaction of a tertiary halide with a tertiary alkoxide, which results exclusively in $E2$ elimination to 2-methylpropene.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What is the Sandmeyer reaction in organic synthesis?

options.text: The replacement of the diazonium group ($-\text{N}_2^+$) in an arenediazonium salt by $-\text{Cl}$, $-\text{Br}$, or $-\text{CN}$ using copper(I) salts as catalysts
The reduction of nitrobenzene to aniline using tin and hydrochloric acid
The conversion of an amide to a primary amine with bromine and alkali
The coupling of two aryl halides with sodium metal in dry ether

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Discovered by Traugott Sandmeyer in 1884, the Sandmeyer reaction uses cuprous salts ($\text{CuCl}$, $\text{CuBr}$, or $\text{CuCN}$) to substitute the diazonium moiety with chloro, bromo, or cyano groups.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What catalyst is typically employed in the Sandmeyer reaction to introduce a chlorine atom onto an aromatic ring?

options.text: Copper(I) chloride dissolved in concentrated hydrochloric acid ($\text{CuCl} / \text{HCl}$)

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: $\text{Ar-N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- \xrightarrow{\text{CuCl}/\text{HCl}} \text{Ar-Cl} + \text{N}_2\uparrow$. $\text{CuCl}$ acts as a single-electron transfer catalyst.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: Which reagents are used in the Sandmeyer reaction to prepare benzonitrile from benzenediazonium chloride?
Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: $\text{Ar-N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- \xrightarrow{\text{CuCN}/\text{KCN}} \text{Ar-CN} + \text{N}_2\uparrow$. This is a crucial method for forming aryl $\text{C-C}$ bonds.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What is the accepted mechanism for the Sandmeyer reaction?

options.text: An electrophilic aromatic substitution via a carbocation intermediate
A radical-nucleophilic process initiated by Single Electron Transfer (SET) from copper(I) to the diazonium cation, generating an aryl radical ($\text{Ar}^\bullet$) and copper(II)

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Mechanism: $\text{Ar-N}_2^+ + \text{Cu}^\text{I}\text{X} \rightarrow \text{Ar}^\bullet + \text{N}_2 + \text{Cu}^\text{II}\text{X}^+$. Then $\text{Ar}^\bullet + \text{Cu}^\text{II}\text{X}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ar-X} + \text{Cu}^\text{I}\text{X}$.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What is the role of copper(I) in the catalytic cycle of the Sandmeyer reaction?

options.text: It acts as a one-electron reducing agent that transfers an electron to the diazonium cation and subsequently transfers the halogen/pseudohalogen back to the aryl radical
It acts as a Lewis acid to cleave the benzene ring
It acts as an oxidizing agent that consumes nitrogen
It absorbs water molecules from the reaction solvent

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Copper alternates between $\text{Cu}^\text{I}$ and $\text{Cu}^\text{II}$ oxidation states, facilitating single-electron reduction to create the aryl radical and then ligand transfer to complete substitution.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: Why is copper(I) catalyst NOT required for the preparation of iodobenzene from benzenediazonium chloride?

options.text: Iodine gas decomposes the diazonium salt spontaneously
Iodide ion ($\text{I}^-$) is a sufficiently powerful reducing agent to directly transfer an electron to the diazonium cation without needing a transition metal catalyst
Iodine is a gas and does not dissolve in water
Copper iodide explodes violently with diazonium salts

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: $\text{I}^-$ has a low oxidation potential (easily oxidized to $\text{I}_2$). Simple warming of the aqueous diazonium solution with $\text{KI}$ affords iodobenzene in high yield: $\text{Ar-N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- + \text{KI} \rightarrow \text{Ar-I} + \text{KCl} + \text{N}_2\uparrow$.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: Why can fluorobenzene NOT be prepared using the classic Sandmeyer reaction with copper(I) fluoride ($\text{CuF}$)?

options.text: Fluorine burns the benzene ring to ashes
Fluorobenzene is unstable and decomposes into acetylene
Fluoride ion has high hydration energy, high oxidation potential, and forms insoluble inactive copper fluorides; fluorobenzene is instead prepared via the Balz-Schiemann reaction using $\text{HBF}_4$
Diazonium ions reject all halogens except iodine

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: The copper(I)/copper(II) redox cycle does not operate effectively with fluoride ligands. Heating diazonium fluoroborate ($\text{ArN}_2^+\text{BF}_4^-$) is used instead (Balz-Schiemann reaction).

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: How does the Gattermann reaction differ from the Sandmeyer reaction?

options.text: The Gattermann reaction uses iron powder instead of copper
The Gattermann reaction prepares only aliphatic amines
The Gattermann reaction requires liquid ammonia
The Gattermann reaction uses finely divided copper powder with $\text{HX}$ instead of cuprous halide ($\text{Cu}_2\text{X}_2 / \text{HX}$)

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: In the Gattermann reaction: $\text{ArN}_2^+\text{X}^- \xrightarrow{\text{Cu powder}/\text{HX}} \text{Ar-X} + \text{N}_2 + \text{CuX}$. It gives slightly lower yields (~40%) than the Sandmeyer reaction (~70-80%).

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: Between the Sandmeyer reaction and the Gattermann reaction, which generally provides superior yields and purity of aryl halides?

options.text: The Sandmeyer reaction gives substantially higher yields and fewer side products because copper(I) halides dissolve to form active homogeneous halocuprate complexes
The Gattermann reaction gives $100\%$ yield while Sandmeyer gives zero
Both reactions give identical yields of less than $5\%$

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Sandmeyer's use of cuprous halides ($\text{CuX}$) provides higher yields (~70–80%) compared to Gattermann's heterogeneous copper powder method (~40%).

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What gas is quantitatively evolved as a thermodynamic driving force in the Sandmeyer reaction?
Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: The formation of the exceptionally stable $\text{N}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bond ($\sim 945\text{ kJ/mol}$ bond enthalpy) provides an enormous thermodynamic driving force (entropy increase and large exothermicity).

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What common side product is formed via dimerization of two aryl radicals during the Sandmeyer reaction?
Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: When two free aryl radicals encounter each other before halogen transfer from $\text{Cu}^\text{II}\text{X}_2$, radical combination produces symmetrical biaryls: $2\text{Ar}^\bullet \rightarrow \text{Ar-Ar}$.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: Why is the Sandmeyer reaction preferred over direct electrophilic aromatic halogenation for preparing $o$-chlorotoluene from toluene?

options.text: Direct chlorination of toluene destroys the benzene ring
Toluene cannot react with chlorine in the presence of $\text{FeCl}_3$

Direct chlorination of toluene produces an inseparable mixture of ortho and para isomers, whereas nitration followed by isomer separation, reduction, diazotization, and Sandmeyer reaction yields pure $o$-chlorotoluene

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: The Sandmeyer pathway allows regiospecific synthesis of pure single positional isomers (such as $o$-chlorotoluene or $m$-bromotoluene) that cannot be obtained purely by direct electrophilic halogenation.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: How can $m$-bromotoluene be synthesized from toluene, given that the methyl group is ortho/para-directing?

options.text: Nitrate toluene $\rightarrow$ separate $p$-nitrotoluene $\rightarrow$ brominate meta to methyl (ortho to nitro) $\rightarrow$ reduce $-\text{NO}_2$ to $-\text{NH}_2$ $\rightarrow$ diazotize $\rightarrow$ deaminate with $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_2$

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Strategic use of the amino/diazonium handle allows removal or replacement at specific positions to generate products inaccessible by direct substitution.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What safety precaution must be taken when performing the Sandmeyer cyanation reaction with $\text{CuCN}$?

options.text: The reaction must be carried out in pure oxygen

The acidic diazonium solution must be neutralized with sodium carbonate before adding the copper(I) cyanide-potassium cyanide complex to prevent evolution of deadly hydrogen cyanide ($\text{HCN}$) gas
The mixture must be heated with an open flame
Liquid sodium must be poured into the flask

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Acidic solutions decompose cyanide salts into lethal volatile $\text{HCN}$ gas: $\text{CN}^- + \text{H}^+ \rightarrow \text{HCN}\uparrow$. Thus, neutralization to neutral or mildly alkaline pH is mandatory.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What is the synthetic utility of converting an arenediazonium salt into a benzonitrile via Sandmeyer cyanation?

options.text: Nitriles cannot undergo any further reactions
The nitrile group always falls off as carbon monoxide

The nitrile group ($-\text{CN}$) introduces a new carbon atom and can be readily hydrolyzed to a carboxylic acid ($-\text{COOH}$), reduced to a primary benzylamine ($-\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$), or converted to an aldehyde ($-\text{CHO}$)
It is only useful for making plastic explosives

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Sandmeyer cyanation is one of the most powerful methods for building benzoic acids, aryl ketones, benzylamines, and aromatic amides from aromatic amines.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What product is obtained when benzenediazonium chloride is treated with $\text{CuCN}/\text{KCN}$, followed by acid-catalyzed hydrolysis ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+, \Delta$)?
Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- \xrightarrow{\text{CuCN}/\text{KCN}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CN} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^+, \Delta} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH} + \text{NH}_4^+$.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What product is obtained when benzonitrile (formed by Sandmeyer cyanation) is reduced with $\text{LiAlH}_4$ or catalytic hydrogenation?
Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Reduction of the cyano group adds four hydrogen atoms across the $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ triple bond: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CN} + 4[\text{H}] \xrightarrow{\text{LiAlH}_4} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: Which of the following describes the oxidation state transformation of copper during the first step of the Sandmeyer mechanism?

options.text: Copper(I) is reduced to metallic Copper(0)
Copper(I) is oxidized to Copper(II) as it transfers an electron to the diazonium cation
Copper remains in the $+3$ oxidation state throughout

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: $\text{Cu}^\text{I} + \text{Ar-N}_2^+ \rightarrow \text{Cu}^\text{II} + \text{Ar}^\bullet + \text{N}_2$. Copper acts as a one-electron donor.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: Which of the following describes the second step of the Sandmeyer catalytic cycle?

options.text: The aryl radical combines with water to form phenol
The aryl radical attacks the benzene ring of another molecule
The aryl radical ($\text{Ar}^\bullet$) abstracts a halogen atom from $\text{Cu}^\text{II}\text{X}_2$, yielding the aryl halide ($\text{Ar-X}$) and regenerating the copper(I) catalyst
Copper is converted permanently to insoluble copper sulfide

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: $\text{Ar}^\bullet + [\text{X-Cu}^\text{II}\text{X}] \rightarrow \text{Ar-X} + \text{Cu}^\text{I}\text{X}$. This ligand-transfer step regenerates $\text{Cu}^\text{I}$.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What spectroscopic technique has been used to detect the transient aryl radical intermediates in the Sandmeyer reaction?

options.text: Electron Paramagnetic Resonance (EPR) spectroscopy / Radical trapping with TEMPO

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Radical scavengers (like TEMPO or acrylonitrile) trap the aryl radical, confirming the single-electron transfer free-radical pathway.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: Can electron-withdrawing groups (such as $-\text{NO}_2$ or $-\text{CF}_3$) on the aromatic ring tolerate the Sandmeyer reaction?

options.text: Yes, the Sandmeyer reaction proceeds smoothly with aromatic rings bearing electron-withdrawing or electron-donating groups
No, electron-withdrawing groups cause spontaneous explosion of the catalyst
No, nitro groups turn into hydroxyl groups
Electron-withdrawing groups convert the diazonium salt into an alkane

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: The Sandmeyer reaction has broad functional group tolerance; both electron-deficient and electron-rich arenediazonium salts undergo efficient substitution.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What is the product when $p$-nitrobenzenediazonium chloride is treated with $\text{CuBr} / \text{HBr}$?
Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: The diazonium group at the 1-position is selectively replaced by bromine, leaving the 4-nitro substituent intact: $p\text{-O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{N}_2^+ + \text{CuBr} \rightarrow p\text{-O}_2\text{N-C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{Br} + \text{N}_2$.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: How is chlorobenzene synthesized commercially in the laboratory starting from nitrobenzene?
Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: This classic 3-step sequence (Reduction $\rightarrow$ Diazotization $\rightarrow$ Sandmeyer) is the textbook route from nitroarenes to haloarenes.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What happens if water is present and the Sandmeyer mixture is warmed without sufficient cuprous halide?

options.text: Phenol is formed as a major byproduct due to competitive heterolytic or homolytic solvolysis by water

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: In the absence of sufficient halide/copper catalyst, diazonium ions hydrolyze upon warming: $\text{Ar-N}_2^+ + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ar-OH} + \text{N}_2 + \text{H}^+$.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What is the primary advantage of the Sandmeyer reaction over direct halogenation for introducing bromine into benzoic acid at the meta position?

options.text: Direct bromination of benzoic acid requires harsh forcing conditions and gives low yields, whereas converting $m$-nitrobenzoic acid via reduction, diazotization, and Sandmeyer reaction gives clean $m$-bromobenzoic acid
Direct bromination gives only ortho-bromobenzoic acid

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: The Sandmeyer approach provides high isomeric purity and mild reaction conditions for substituted aryl halides.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What is the formula of cuprous chloride used in the Sandmeyer reaction?
Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Cuprous chloride has copper in the $+1$ oxidation state and exists as a tetrahedral cluster/dimer $\text{Cu}_2\text{Cl}_2$ in the crystalline and solution state.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: Why is $\text{HCl}$ used in conjunction with $\text{CuCl}$ in the Sandmeyer chlorination?

options.text: $\text{CuCl}$ is virtually insoluble in pure water; concentrated $\text{HCl}$ dissolves it by forming soluble chlorocuprate(I) complex ions such as $[\text{CuCl}_2]^-$ and $[\text{CuCl}_3]^{2-}$

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Cuprous chloride dissolves readily in concentrated $\text{HCl}$ via complex ion formation: $\text{CuCl} + \text{Cl}^- \rightleftharpoons [\text{CuCl}_2]^-$, ensuring a homogeneous and active catalytic species.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: In the preparation of $o$-bromotoluene from $o$-toluidine via the Sandmeyer reaction, what are the sequential reagents?
Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: $o$-Toluidine is diazotized with nitrous acid and hydrobromic acid at ice-cold temperature, followed by addition of cuprous bromide in hydrobromic acid to yield $o$-bromotoluene.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: Which of the following haloarenes CANNOT be prepared by the Sandmeyer reaction?

options.text: None; all three can be prepared

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Fluorobenzene cannot be prepared by the Sandmeyer reaction; it is synthesized by the Balz-Schiemann reaction.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What is the oxidation state of copper in $\text{CuCN}$?
Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Copper is in the cuprous state ($	ext{Cu}^+$) with a $\text{d}^{10}$ electron configuration.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: Why is the Sandmeyer reaction categorized as an organometallic radical reaction?

options.text: Because a transition metal ($\text{Cu}^\text{I}$) mediates the formation and transfer of free radical intermediates without generating free carbanions or benzyne
Because copper metal is melted into liquid

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: The discovery of copper-catalyzed radical generation from diazonium salts helped pioneer modern transition-metal-catalyzed cross-coupling and radical chemistry.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: How does the reactivity of arenediazonium salts in the Sandmeyer reaction compare to that of aliphatic diazonium salts?

options.text: Aliphatic diazonium salts give higher yields than aromatic ones
Both are stable at room temperature for months
Arenediazonium salts are sufficiently stable at $0-5^\circ\text{C}$ to participate in the Sandmeyer reaction, whereas aliphatic diazonium salts decompose uncontrollably within picoseconds

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Aliphatic diazonium ions undergo instantaneous loss of $\text{N}_2$ to yield carbocation rearrangements and mixtures; only aromatic diazonium salts are stable enough for the Sandmeyer reaction.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What happens if a Sandmeyer chlorination is carried out using $\text{CuSO}_4 + \text{NaCl}$ without a reducing agent?

options.text: Reaction fails or gives low yields because $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ (copper(II)) cannot initiate the single-electron transfer reduction of the diazonium cation

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: The active catalyst is $\text{Cu}^\text{I}$, not $\text{Cu}^\text{II}$. If copper(II) sulfate is used, it must first be reduced to $\text{Cu}^\text{I}$ with sodium sulfite or copper turnings.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What reagent mixture is commonly used to freshly prepare cuprous chloride solution in the laboratory?
Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Copper(II) is reduced to copper(I) by sulfite: $2\text{Cu}^{2+} + 2\text{Cl}^- + \text{SO}_3^{2-} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow 2\text{CuCl}\downarrow + \text{SO}_4^{2-} + 2\text{H}^+$.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What is the product when $p$-toluidine undergoes diazotization followed by treatment with $\text{CuCN} / \text{KCN}$?
Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: The diazonium group of $p$-methylbenzenediazonium chloride is replaced by $-\text{CN}$, producing $p$-tolunitrile.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What is the byproduct gas released when arenediazonium chloride is warmed with copper powder and $\text{HCl}$ in the Gattermann reaction?
Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Both Sandmeyer and Gattermann reactions expel dinitrogen gas ($\text{N}_2$) quantitatively as the diazonium group is replaced.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: Why is potassium iodide ($\text{KI}$) simply added to the cold diazonium solution without any copper salt to prepare iodobenzene?

options.text: Because $\text{I}^-$ is easily oxidized to $\text{I}^\bullet$ by $[\text{Ar-N}_2]^+$, generating the aryl radical and iodine atoms that combine to give $\text{Ar-I}$
Because iodine boils at low temperatures
Because potassium forms an explosive alloy with copper
Because diazonium iodide is completely insoluble

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: The reduction potential of diazonium cation ($E^\circ \approx +0.45\text{ V}$) is high enough to be directly reduced by iodide ($E^\circ(\text{I}_2/\text{I}^-) = +0.54\text{ V}$), rendering copper catalyst unnecessary.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds can be synthesized from aniline via a Sandmeyer reaction followed by alkaline hydrolysis?

options.text: Phenol (if hydrolyzed directly) or Benzoic acid (if converted to benzonitrile then hydrolyzed)

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Sequence: Aniline $\rightarrow$ Benzenediazonium salt $\xrightarrow{\text{CuCN}/\text{KCN}}$ Benzonitrile $\xrightarrow{\text{OH}^-, \Delta, \text{H}^+}$ Benzoic acid.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What is the effect of replacing $\text{CuCl}$ with $\text{CuBr}$ in the Sandmeyer reaction?

options.text: A nitro group is introduced instead
The reaction introduces a bromine atom instead of a chlorine atom onto the aromatic ring

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: The nature of the halogen transferred to the aryl radical depends entirely on the cuprous halide employed ($\text{CuCl} \rightarrow \text{Ar-Cl}$; $\text{CuBr} \rightarrow \text{Ar-Br}$).

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: When benzenediazonium chloride is treated with $\text{CuCl} / \text{HCl}$ in the presence of an alkene (such as styrene or acrylic acid), what reaction occurs instead?

options.text: Meerwein Arylation (radical addition of the aryl group and chlorine across the double bond of the alkene)

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: In the presence of alkenes, the copper-generated aryl radical attacks the $\text{C=C}$ double bond, followed by chlorine transfer from $\text{CuCl}_2$; this is known as the Meerwein arylation.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: Why does the Sandmeyer reaction require an acidic environment for chlorination and bromination?

options.text: Acid prevents the decomposition of the arenediazonium salt into diazotate or phenol and stabilizes the chlorocuprate(I) species
Acid turns the benzene ring into a gas
Acid causes precipitation of metallic copper

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: At neutral or basic pH, diazonium ions hydrolyze or convert to unreactive diazotates, and cuprous halides precipitate as unreactive copper(I) oxide ($\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$).

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What is the thermal stability of dry benzenediazonium chloride?

options.text: It is violently explosive when dry and must never be isolated; it is always handled in cold aqueous solution
It is a liquid that freezes at $100^\circ\text{C}$

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Dry arenediazonium halides are shock- and heat-sensitive primary explosives. Sandmeyer reactions are always carried out in situ without isolating the dry salt.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: In the synthesis of saccharin (an artificial sweetener), which reaction is used to convert 2-aminobenzoic acid methyl ester into the corresponding sulfonyl chloride via diazotization?

options.text: A modified Sandmeyer-type sulfochlorination using $\text{SO}_2$ and $\text{CuCl}_2$ (Meerwein-Sandmeyer sulfochlorination)

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: Treatment of diazonium salts with $\text{SO}_2$ in the presence of $\text{CuCl}$ yields arylsulfonyl chlorides ($\text{Ar-SO}_2\text{Cl}$), a valuable variant of the Sandmeyer reaction.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What happens when an arenediazonium salt is treated with $\text{Cu(NO}_2)_2$ in the presence of $\text{Cu}_2\text{O}$ or $\text{Cu}$ powder?

options.text: The ring expands into a seven-membered tropylium cation
The diazonium group is replaced by a nitro group ($-\text{NO}_2$), yielding a nitroarene

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: A modified Sandmeyer reaction using sodium nitrite and cuprous oxide introduces a nitro group, useful for synthesizing nitro compounds inaccessible by direct nitration.

Sandmeyer Reaction.question: What is the general yield and synthetic importance of the Sandmeyer reaction in modern pharmaceutical chemistry?

options.text: Yields typically exceed $70-85\%$; it is an indispensable tool for introducing halogen and nitrile handles for subsequent transition-metal-catalyzed cross-couplings (Suzuki, Heck, Buchwald)
Yields are less than $1\%$, making it obsolete
It is only used for making inorganic minerals
It converts all pharmaceuticals into toxic cyanide

Sandmeyer Reaction.explanation: The aryl halides and benzonitriles produced by the Sandmeyer reaction are fundamental building blocks for carbon-carbon and carbon-heteroatom bond construction in medicinal chemistry.

Gattermann Reaction.question: What reagents are used in the Gattermann reaction for preparing haloarenes from arenediazonium salts?

options.text: Finely divided copper powder ($\text{Cu}$) and concentrated halogen acid ($\text{HCl}$ or $\text{HBr}$)
Potassium iodide in aqueous solution without catalyst

Gattermann Reaction.explanation: The Gattermann reaction employs freshly prepared arenediazonium chloride with copper powder and concentrated halogen acid: $\text{ArN}_2^+\text{Cl}^- \xrightarrow{\text{Cu} / \text{HCl}} \text{ArCl} + \text{N}_2 + \text{CuCl}$.

Gattermann Reaction.question: How does the Gattermann reaction differ from the Sandmeyer reaction for preparing chlorobenzene?

options.text: Gattermann produces bromobenzene only, while Sandmeyer produces chlorobenzene only
Gattermann uses metallic copper powder ($\text{Cu}$), whereas Sandmeyer uses cuprous salts ($\text{Cu}_2\text{Cl}_2$)
Gattermann uses sodium nitrite, whereas Sandmeyer uses nitric acid
Gattermann does not liberate nitrogen gas

Gattermann Reaction.explanation: The key distinction is the catalyst: Sandmeyer uses copper(I) salts ($\text{Cu}_2\text{Cl}_2 / \text{Cu}_2\text{Br}_2$), whereas Gattermann uses metallic copper powder ($\text{Cu}$) in presence of halogen acid.

Gattermann Reaction.question: How do the yields of haloarenes in the Gattermann reaction compare to those in the Sandmeyer reaction?

options.text: The Gattermann reaction gives 100% yield while Sandmeyer gives less than 10%
Both reactions always give identical yields
The Sandmeyer reaction generally gives higher yields (approx. 70-80%) than the Gattermann reaction (approx. 40-50%)
Gattermann reaction fails completely for chlorobenzene

Gattermann Reaction.explanation: Due to the homogeneous nature and efficient electron transfer of cuprous complexes, Sandmeyer's method is synthetically superior with higher yields than the heterogeneous copper powder method of Gattermann.

Gattermann Reaction.question: What gas is evolved during the Gattermann reaction?
Gattermann Reaction.explanation: The diazonium group is an exceptional leaving group that is expelled as thermodynamically stable nitrogen gas: $\text{ArN}_2^+ \rightarrow \text{Ar}^\bullet + \text{N}_2\uparrow$.

Gattermann Reaction.question: What is the primary driving force for the Gattermann reaction?

options.text: The thermodynamic stability of molecular nitrogen ($\text{N}_2$) and the high entropy gain upon its gas evolution
The strong oxidizing power of copper

Gattermann Reaction.explanation: Evolution of molecular nitrogen with its exceptionally strong triple bond ($N\equiv N$, $945\text{ kJ/mol}$) and large positive entropy change ($\Delta S > 0$) drives the reaction irreversibly forward.

Gattermann Reaction.question: What is the major organic product when benzenediazonium chloride is treated with copper powder and hydrobromic acid ($\text{HBr}$)?
Gattermann Reaction.explanation: Reaction of benzenediazonium chloride with $Cu$ and $HBr$ replaces the diazonium group with bromine, producing bromobenzene and releasing $N_2$.

Gattermann Reaction.question: What is the active mechanism of the Gattermann reaction on the copper metal surface?

options.text: Bimolecular nucleophilic substitution ($S_N2$) with Walden inversion
Single-electron transfer (SET) from metallic copper to the diazonium cation to form an aryl radical ($\text{Ar}^\bullet$)
