Wolff-Kishner Reduction.question: When 4-phenylbutan-2-one is treated with $\text{NH}_2\text{NH}_2 / \text{KOH}$ in ethylene glycol at $470\text{ K}$, the product is:
Wolff-Kishner Reduction.explanation: Deoxygenation of the C-2 carbonyl gives 1-phenylbutane.

Wolff-Kishner Reduction.question: Why is an excess of hydrazine hydrate typically used in the Huang-Minlon procedure?

options.text: To act as the primary solvent
To ensure complete conversion of the carbonyl compound to hydrazone and prevent azine formation ($>\text{C}=\text{N}-\text{N}=\text{C}<$)

Wolff-Kishner Reduction.explanation: Excess hydrazine suppresses the secondary condensation of hydrazone with unreacted carbonyl compound to form an insoluble azine.

Wolff-Kishner Reduction.question: What happens when an $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated ketone is reduced under Wolff-Kishner conditions?

options.text: Only the double bond is reduced while carbonyl stays intact
The molecule undergoes cleavage to two carboxylic acids
The carbonyl is reduced to methylene, and double-bond migration or pyrazoline formation can occur depending on conditions

Wolff-Kishner Reduction.explanation: Hydrazones of $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated ketones can cyclize to form pyrazolines, which decompose to cyclopropanes or alkenes upon heating.

Wolff-Kishner Reduction.question: What is the product when 2-adamantanone is treated with hydrazine and $\text{KOH}$ in diethylene glycol?
Wolff-Kishner Reduction.explanation: The bridgehead-flanked ketone carbonyl of 2-adamantanone is cleanly reduced to methylene, yielding adamantane.

Wolff-Kishner Reduction.question: Which of the following compounds gives toluene upon Wolff-Kishner reduction?

options.text: Both Benzaldehyde and Benzophenone (wait, benzaldehyde only!)

Wolff-Kishner Reduction.explanation: Benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$) is reduced to toluene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$). Benzophenone yields diphenylmethane.

Wolff-Kishner Reduction.question: Identify the gas that extinguishes a burning splint evolved during the second step of Wolff-Kishner reduction:
Wolff-Kishner Reduction.explanation: Molecular nitrogen gas ($\text{N}_2$) is an inert gas that extinguishes a flame.

Wolff-Kishner Reduction.question: What is the effect of having an ester group on the same molecule during Wolff-Kishner reduction?

options.text: The ester is reduced to an alkane
The ester is reduced to an ether
The ester undergoes saponification by $\text{KOH}$ to form a carboxylate salt

Wolff-Kishner Reduction.explanation: Under hot concentrated alkaline conditions, ester bonds are rapidly saponified to carboxylate salts.

Wolff-Kishner Reduction.question: What is the final organic product when acetophenone is treated with $\text{NH}_2\text{NH}_2 / \text{KOH}$ in ethylene glycol followed by heating?
Wolff-Kishner Reduction.explanation: Acetophenone is deoxygenated cleanly to ethylbenzene.

Etard Reaction.question: Which reagent is characteristically used in the Etard Reaction for converting toluene to benzaldehyde?
Etard Reaction.explanation: The Etard reaction uses chromyl chloride ($\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$) in non-polar solvents like $\text{CS}_2$ or $\text{CCl}_4$, followed by hydrolysis.

Etard Reaction.question: What is the brown-colored solid intermediate formed during the Etard reaction of toluene before hydrolysis?
Etard Reaction.explanation: Reaction of toluene with two moles of chromyl chloride produces a brown, insoluble chromium complex of formula $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(OCrOHCl}_2)_2$.

Etard Reaction.question: What is the final organic product obtained after aqueous hydrolysis of the Etard chromium complex?
Etard Reaction.explanation: Hydrolysis of the brown chromium complex with water cleaves the chromium-oxygen bonds, liberating benzaldehyde cleanly.

Etard Reaction.question: Why does the oxidation in the Etard reaction stop at the aldehyde stage rather than continuing to benzoic acid?

options.text: Because chromyl chloride is a reducing agent
Because benzaldehyde is insoluble in water
Because the reaction is run at absolute zero
Because the intermediate chromium complex precipitates out as an insoluble solid in non-polar solvent ($\text{CS}_2$), protecting it from further oxidation

Etard Reaction.explanation: Formation of the insoluble coordination complex isolates the benzylic carbon from further oxidation; subsequent mild hydrolysis releases the aldehyde.

Etard Reaction.question: Which of the following non-polar solvents is most commonly used in the Etard reaction?
Etard Reaction.explanation: Inert, non-polar, aprotic solvents like $\text{CS}_2$, $\text{CCl}_4$, or chloroform are used to dissolve $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$ without reacting with it.

Etard Reaction.question: What is the oxidation state of chromium in chromyl chloride ($\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$)?
Etard Reaction.explanation: In $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$, oxygen is -2 and chlorine is -1. Thus $x + 2(-2) + 2(-1) = 0 \implies x = +6$.

Etard Reaction.question: When p-xylene (1,4-dimethylbenzene) is treated with chromyl chloride followed by hydrolysis, the product formed by partial oxidation is:
Etard Reaction.explanation: Controlled Etard oxidation selectively oxidizes one methyl group to formyl, yielding 4-methylbenzaldehyde.

Etard Reaction.question: What is the physical state and color of chromyl chloride ($\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$)?
Etard Reaction.explanation: Chromyl chloride is a dark red, volatile, fuming liquid ($b.p. \approx 117^\circ\text{C}$) that fumes in moist air.

Etard Reaction.question: What happens if water is added directly to the initial mixture before the reaction between toluene and $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$ completes?

options.text: Chromyl chloride vigorously hydrolyzes to chromic acid and hydrochloric acid, ruining the reaction

Etard Reaction.explanation: Chromyl chloride is violently moisture-sensitive: $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{CrO}_4 + 2\text{HCl}$.

Etard Reaction.question: When ethylbenzene is subjected to the Etard reaction, what is the major carbonyl product formed?
Etard Reaction.explanation: Chromyl chloride oxidizes the secondary benzylic carbon of ethylbenzene to a ketone carbonyl, yielding acetophenone.

Etard Reaction.question: Why does oxidation with acidic $\text{KMnO}_4$ fail to give benzaldehyde from toluene, whereas the Etard reaction succeeds?

options.text: $\text{KMnO}_4$ is a very strong oxidizing agent that oxidizes toluene uncontrollably all the way to benzoic acid

Etard Reaction.explanation: Acidic or alkaline $\text{KMnO}_4$ vigorously oxidizes benzylic carbons past the aldehyde stage directly to carboxylate (benzoic acid).

Etard Reaction.question: What is the molar ratio of toluene to $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$ required to form the brown intermediate complex?
Etard Reaction.explanation: Two molecules of $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$ add per molecule of toluene: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3 + 2\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2 \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(OCrOHCl}_2)_2$.

Etard Reaction.question: In the preparation of benzaldehyde from toluene using $\text{CrO}_3$ in acetic anhydride (a related commercial alternative to Etard reaction), what intermediate is formed?
Etard Reaction.explanation: Acetic anhydride traps benzaldehyde in situ as a stable gem-diacetate (benzylidene diacetate), preventing over-oxidation; acid hydrolysis regenerates benzaldehyde.

Etard Reaction.question: What is the product when 4-chlorotoluene is subjected to the Etard reaction?
Etard Reaction.explanation: The methyl group is oxidized cleanly to a formyl group while the aryl chlorine remains intact, giving 4-chlorobenzaldehyde.

Etard Reaction.question: What type of reaction mechanism is involved in the formation of the Etard complex?

options.text: Ene reaction followed by $[2,3]$-sigmatropic rearrangement involving the $\text{Cr}=\text{O}$ bond

Etard Reaction.explanation: Mechanistic studies show that chromyl chloride reacts via an initial ene-type reaction with the benzylic $\text{C-H}$ bond followed by a $[2,3]$-sigmatropic shift.

Etard Reaction.question: What is the product when propylbenzene is treated with $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2 / \text{CS}_2$ followed by hydrolysis?
Etard Reaction.explanation: Chromyl chloride selectively attacks the benzylic methylene position, oxidizing it to a ketone (propiophenone).

Etard Reaction.question: Why is carbon disulfide ($\text{CS}_2$) chosen as the solvent despite being flammable?

options.text: Because it is completely inert toward chromyl chloride and does not undergo oxidation or electrophilic chlorination under reaction conditions
Because it has a boiling point of $500^\circ\text{C}$
Because it acts as a base

Etard Reaction.explanation: $\text{CS}_2$ is resistant to oxidation by $\text{Cr(VI)}$ and provides a non-polar medium from which the brown complex precipitates immediately.

Etard Reaction.question: When 2-nitrotoluene is subjected to the Etard reaction, what is the product?
Etard Reaction.explanation: The benzylic methyl group is oxidized to formyl, yielding 2-nitrobenzaldehyde.

Etard Reaction.question: What is the color of the reaction mixture when chromyl chloride is first mixed with toluene in $\text{CS}_2$?
Etard Reaction.explanation: The Etard complex precipitates out as a characteristic chocolate-brown amorphous solid.

Etard Reaction.question: What reducing agent is often added during the aqueous hydrolysis step of the Etard reaction to prevent oxidation by any remaining hexavalent chromium?
Etard Reaction.explanation: Aqueous sodium bisulfite or sodium sulfite reduces any excess unreacted $\text{Cr(VI)}$ to $\text{Cr(III)}$, preventing inadvertent over-oxidation of the liberated benzaldehyde.

Etard Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds CANNOT be prepared by the Etard reaction?
Etard Reaction.explanation: The Etard reaction requires a benzylic $\text{C-H}$ bond activated by an adjacent aromatic ring; simple aliphatic alkanes like ethane do not react selectively.

Etard Reaction.question: What is the oxidation state of chromium in the final aqueous waste after bisulfite reduction?
Etard Reaction.explanation: Hexavalent chromium is reduced to stable trivalent chromium ($\text{Cr}^{3+}$, green solution) during workup.

Etard Reaction.question: In the Etard reaction of toluene, what is the role of the aromatic ring?

options.text: It provides steric hindrance to prevent oxidation
It stabilizes the developing radical/cationic charge at the benzylic position through resonance, activating the benzylic $\text{C-H}$ bonds

Etard Reaction.explanation: The aromatic ring significantly lowers the benzylic $\text{C-H}$ bond dissociation energy ($BDE \approx 375\text{ kJ/mol}$ vs $420\text{ kJ/mol}$ in methane), enabling facile attack.

Etard Reaction.question: What happens when diphenylmethane ($(\text{C}_6\text{H}_5)_2\text{CH}_2$) is treated with $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$ followed by hydrolysis?
Etard Reaction.explanation: The benzylic methylene carbon between the two phenyl rings is oxidized to a ketone carbonyl, yielding benzophenone.

Etard Reaction.question: What is the product when 1-methylnaphthalene is subjected to the Etard reaction?
Etard Reaction.explanation: The benzylic methyl group on the naphthalene ring is oxidized to formyl, yielding 1-naphthaldehyde.

Etard Reaction.question: How does the Etard reaction differ from side-chain chlorination followed by hydrolysis for making benzaldehyde?

options.text: Etard reaction uses $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$ without chlorine gas, avoiding contamination by ring-chlorinated isomers
Side-chain chlorination produces benzyl alcohol exclusively
Etard reaction produces toluene from benzaldehyde

Etard Reaction.explanation: Side-chain chlorination ($\text{Cl}_2/h\nu$) often leads to poly-chlorination and ring substitution byproducts; Etard reaction is highly selective for the aldehyde.

Etard Reaction.question: What is the formula of chromyl chloride?
Etard Reaction.explanation: Chromyl chloride is the inorganic coordination compound $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$.

Etard Reaction.question: In the chromyl chloride test for chloride ions, which red vapors are produced that are identical to the Etard reagent?
Etard Reaction.explanation: Heating a chloride salt with $\text{K}_2\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7$ and conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ evolves red vapors of chromyl chloride ($\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$).

Etard Reaction.question: What is the product when 4-methoxytoluene is subjected to the Etard reaction?
Etard Reaction.explanation: Oxidation of the 4-methyl group yields 4-methoxybenzaldehyde (anisaldehyde).

Etard Reaction.question: Why does tert-butylbenzene NOT react under Etard reaction conditions?

options.text: Because tert-butyl is an electron withdrawing group
Because the benzylic carbon has NO benzylic hydrogens ($\alpha$-hydrogens)
Because the aromatic ring is destroyed

Etard Reaction.explanation: Oxidation requires at least one benzylic hydrogen to undergo hydrogen abstraction; tert-butylbenzene has none.

Etard Reaction.question: Which of the following describes the change in oxidation number of the benzylic carbon in toluene ($-3$) when converted to benzaldehyde?

options.text: Oxidation number changes from -3 to +1 (loss of 4 electrons)

Etard Reaction.explanation: In toluene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_3$), the benzylic carbon has 3 bonds to H ($-3$) and one to C ($0$), so state is $-3$. In benzaldehyde ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$), it has one bond to C ($0$), one to H ($-1$), and two to O ($+2$), so state is $+1$. Net change is $+4$.

Etard Reaction.question: When 3,4-dimethoxytoluene is subjected to Etard oxidation, the product is:
Etard Reaction.explanation: Oxidation of the methyl group of 3,4-dimethoxytoluene gives veratraldehyde.

Etard Reaction.question: What happens when mesitylene (1,3,5-trimethylbenzene) is treated with 1 equivalent of $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$?
Etard Reaction.explanation: Controlled stoichiometry oxidizes one of the three equivalent methyl groups to formyl, yielding 3,5-dimethylbenzaldehyde.

Etard Reaction.question: What is the main safety precaution when handling chromyl chloride in the laboratory?

options.text: It must be kept in direct sunlight to prevent explosion
It is a volatile, corrosive, carcinogenic oxidizer that reacts violently with organic matter and must be handled in a fume hood
It should be tasted to verify purity
It must be dissolved in gasoline

Etard Reaction.explanation: Chromyl chloride is an extremely hazardous $\text{Cr(VI)}$ carcinogen and potent oxidizer requiring strict inert atmosphere/fume hood handling.

Etard Reaction.question: What is the product when 2-chlorotoluene undergoes Etard reaction?
Etard Reaction.explanation: The ortho-methyl group is converted to formyl, giving 2-chlorobenzaldehyde.

Etard Reaction.question: Which of the following statements about the Etard reaction is FALSE?

options.text: It forms a brown chromium complex as an intermediate
Hydrolysis of the intermediate yields benzaldehyde
It oxidizes toluene directly to benzoic acid without stopping at the aldehyde

Etard Reaction.explanation: Statement 1 is false: the entire synthetic hallmark of the Etard reaction is stopping precisely at the aldehyde stage.

Etard Reaction.question: In the Etard reaction, the chromium atom in the brown complex is bonded directly to:

options.text: The benzylic carbon directly via a $\text{C-Cr}$ covalent bond

Etard Reaction.explanation: The structure is $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH(OCrOHCl}_2)_2$, where the benzylic carbon is bonded to oxygen, which is coordinated to chromium.

Etard Reaction.question: When isopropylbenzene (cumene) is treated with chromyl chloride, what is the primary carbonyl product formed?
Etard Reaction.explanation: The tertiary benzylic carbon is attacked; subsequent fragmentation/rearrangement gives acetophenone and related carbonyls.

Etard Reaction.question: How can benzaldehyde obtained from the Etard reaction be purified from residual chromium species?

options.text: By washing the organic extract with aqueous sodium bisulfite solution to form the water-soluble bisulfite adduct, separating, and regenerating with dilute acid

Etard Reaction.explanation: Benzaldehyde forms a crystalline, water-soluble sodium bisulfite addition compound, allowing complete separation from non-carbonyl impurities before regeneration.

Etard Reaction.question: What is the formal valence of oxygen in the chromyl chloride molecule?
Etard Reaction.explanation: The two oxo ligands in $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$ have standard oxidation states of -2 each.

Etard Reaction.question: Which of the following name reactions converts toluene directly into benzaldehyde in a single step?
Etard Reaction.explanation: Etard reaction directly oxidizes toluene to benzaldehyde using $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2$.

Etard Reaction.question: Why is acetic acid NOT used as the solvent in the Etard reaction with chromyl chloride?

options.text: Acetic acid can react with chromyl chloride or lead to uncontrolled over-oxidation to benzoic acid
Toluene is insoluble in acetic acid
Acetic acid precipitates as a gas

Etard Reaction.explanation: Protic solvents like acetic acid facilitate rapid solvolysis and premature breakdown of the protective chromium complex, leading to over-oxidation.

Etard Reaction.question: When 4-bromotoluene is treated with $\text{CrO}_2\text{Cl}_2 / \text{CS}_2$ followed by $\text{H}_2\text{O}$, the product is:
Etard Reaction.explanation: The benzylic methyl group is oxidized to formyl, yielding 4-bromobenzaldehyde.

Etard Reaction.question: Identify reagent $A$ in: $\text{Toluene} \xrightarrow{A} \text{Brown complex} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^+} \text{Benzaldehyde}$:
Etard Reaction.explanation: The reagent combination is chromyl chloride in carbon disulfide (Etard reagent).

Etard Reaction.question: What is the key commercial value of the Etard reaction in the fragrance and flavor industry?

options.text: Direct high-purity synthesis of benzaldehyde (almond aroma) free from chlorinated contaminants

Etard Reaction.explanation: Benzaldehyde synthesized via the Etard route is chlorine-free and safe for use as bitter almond food flavoring and cosmetic perfume.

Stephen Reaction.question: Which reagent combination is used in the Stephen Reaction for reducing nitriles to aldehydes?

options.text: Stannous chloride ($\text{SnCl}_2$) and concentrated $\text{HCl}$, followed by hydrolysis with warm water

Stephen Reaction.explanation: The Stephen reaction involves the reduction of an alkyl or aryl nitrile with $\text{SnCl}_2$ and concentrated $\text{HCl}$ in ether, followed by hydrolysis of the resulting aldimine hydrochloride with warm water.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the intermediate formed during the Stephen reduction before aqueous hydrolysis?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: Reduction of the nitrile triple bond by $\text{SnCl}_2/\text{HCl}$ yields an aldimine hydrochloride ($R-\text{CH}=\text{NH}_2^+\text{Cl}^-$) as a crystalline precipitate.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the final organic product when ethanenitrile (acetonitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CN}$) is subjected to the Stephen Reaction?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: $\text{CH}_3\text{CN} \xrightarrow{1.\; \text{SnCl}_2 + \text{HCl}} \text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{NH}\cdot\text{HCl} \xrightarrow{2.\; \text{H}_2\text{O, } \Delta} \text{CH}_3\text{CHO} + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the final organic product formed when benzonitrile ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CN}$) undergoes Stephen reduction?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: Benzonitrile is reduced to benzaldehyde by $\text{SnCl}_2/\text{HCl}$ followed by aqueous hydrolysis.

Stephen Reaction.question: What inorganic by-product of tin is formed during the Stephen reduction step?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: Tin(II) is oxidized to tin(IV): $\text{Sn}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+} + 2\text{e}^-$. $\text{SnCl}_2 + 2\text{HCl} \rightarrow \text{H}_2\text{SnCl}_4$ / $\text{SnCl}_4$.

Stephen Reaction.question: Which modern organometallic reagent can also selectively reduce nitriles to aldehydes, acting as an alternative to the Stephen reaction?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: DIBAL-H reduces nitriles selectively to imines at low temperatures ($-78^\circ\text{C}$), which on hydrolysis yield aldehydes cleanly.

Stephen Reaction.question: Why is anhydrous ether or ethyl acetate saturated with dry $\text{HCl}$ gas used as the solvent in the Stephen reaction?

options.text: Because water accelerates the reduction of tin
To precipitate the aldimine hydrochloride as a stable crystalline complex and prevent premature hydrolysis
Because ether acts as a reducing agent

Stephen Reaction.explanation: Anhydrous conditions ensure that the aldimine salt precipitates as an insoluble complex without undergoing uncontrolled premature hydrolysis in acid.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the oxidation state of tin in the reducing agent of the Stephen reaction?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: Stannous chloride is $\text{SnCl}_2$, where tin has an oxidation state of +2.

Stephen Reaction.question: What inorganic ammonium salt is produced during the aqueous hydrolysis step of the Stephen reaction?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: Hydrolysis of the aldimine hydrochloride with water yields the aldehyde and ammonium chloride: $R\text{CH}=\text{NH}\cdot\text{HCl} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow R\text{CHO} + \text{NH}_4\text{Cl}$.

Stephen Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds CANNOT be reduced to an aldehyde by the Stephen reaction?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: The Stephen reaction is specifically an aldehyde synthesis from nitriles; nitrobenzene lacks a nitrile group and instead reduces to aniline.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the product when propionitrile ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$) undergoes Stephen reduction?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: Reduction of the cyano group in propionitrile yields propanal.

Stephen Reaction.question: Why does the Stephen reaction stop at the aldimine stage without reducing further to a primary amine under standard conditions?

options.text: Because $\text{SnCl}_2$ is too strong an oxidizing agent
Because primary amines are less stable than imines
Because nitriles do not possess enough electrons
Because the aldimine precipitates out of the anhydrous ethereal reaction mixture as an insoluble crystalline hydrochloride salt

Stephen Reaction.explanation: The aldimine salt $(\text{RCH}=\text{NH}_2^+\text{Cl}^-)$ is insoluble in dry ether and precipitates, protecting it from further reduction to amine.

Stephen Reaction.question: When phenylacetonitrile ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$) is subjected to the Stephen reaction, the product obtained is:
Stephen Reaction.explanation: The cyano carbon is converted into a formyl group without cleaving the benzylic carbon-carbon bond, yielding phenylacetaldehyde.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the number of electrons transferred by $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ to the nitrile carbon in the Stephen reduction?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: The half reaction is $\text{Sn}^{2+} \rightarrow \text{Sn}^{4+} + 2\text{e}^-$, transferring two electrons to the nitrile bond.

Stephen Reaction.question: What compound is formed when 4-cyanotoluene is treated with $\text{SnCl}_2 / \text{HCl}$ followed by warm water?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: The cyano group at the para-position is converted to an aldehyde group, giving 4-methylbenzaldehyde.

Stephen Reaction.question: Which of the following describes the nature of the aldimine intermediate in the Stephen reaction?

options.text: A Schiff base salt ($[R-\text{CH}=\text{NH}_2]^+\text{Cl}^-$) that undergoes nucleophilic addition of water

Stephen Reaction.explanation: The aldimine is a protonated imine (Schiff base conjugate acid) susceptible to rapid nucleophilic addition of water to form a carbinolamine that expels $\text{NH}_4^+$.

Stephen Reaction.question: Consider the sequence: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{KCN / aq. ethanol}} A \xrightarrow{\text{SnCl}_2 / \text{HCl, then } \text{H}_2\text{O}} B$. What is $B$?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: Benzyl bromide undergoes nucleophilic substitution with $\text{KCN}$ to give phenylacetonitrile ($A$), which undergoes Stephen reduction to give phenylacetaldehyde ($B$).

Stephen Reaction.question: In the Stephen reaction of butanenitrile, what is the chemical formula of the final aldehyde?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: Butanenitrile has 4 carbons ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CN}$); its reduction yields the 4-carbon aldehyde butanal.

Stephen Reaction.question: Why is DIBAL-H often favored industrially over the classic Stephen reaction?

options.text: DIBAL-H is cheaper than table salt
DIBAL-H produces higher yields without generating heavy metal tin-waste sludges and operates smoothly on both nitriles and esters

Stephen Reaction.explanation: The Stephen reaction produces stoichiometric toxic tin byproducts ($\{\text{SnCl}_4, \text{Sn(OH)}_4\}$), whereas DIBAL-H produces easily manageable aluminium salts.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the product when 1-cyanonaphthalene is treated with $\text{SnCl}_2 / \text{HCl}$ followed by hydrolysis?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: The 1-cyano group is converted to 1-formyl, yielding 1-naphthaldehyde.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the role of steam distillation in the work-up of the Stephen reaction?

options.text: To co-distill the volatile aldehyde away from non-volatile tin salts and ammonium chloride
To oxidize the aldehyde to acid

Stephen Reaction.explanation: Steam distillation efficiently separates steam-volatile aldehydes (e.g. benzaldehyde) from aqueous, inorganic tin salts.

Stephen Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds gives 2-methylbutanal via Stephen reduction?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: Reduction of 2-methylbutanenitrile, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH(CH}_3)\text{CN}$, yields 2-methylbutanal.

Stephen Reaction.question: What happens if concentrated nitric acid is used instead of concentrated $\text{HCl}$ in the Stephen reaction?

options.text: The reaction rate increases a thousand-fold
Alkanes are formed instead of aldehydes
The reaction fails because nitric acid oxidizes $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ immediately to $\text{Sn}^{4+}$ and oxidizes the organic substrate
No effect, as all acids are identical

Stephen Reaction.explanation: Nitric acid is a powerful oxidizing agent that would instantly oxidize $\text{SnCl}_2$ and destroy the nitrile substrate.

Stephen Reaction.question: What type of organic functional group is the starting material of the Stephen reaction?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: The Stephen reaction exclusively utilizes nitriles as the starting material.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the bond order between carbon and nitrogen in the aldimine intermediate of Stephen reaction?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: Reduction of the nitrile triple bond ($\,\text{C}\equiv\text{N}\,$, bond order 3) yields the aldimine ($\,\text{C}=\text{N}\,$, bond order 2).

Stephen Reaction.question: Consider: $\text{CH}_3\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{KCN}} A \xrightarrow{\text{SnCl}_2 / \text{HCl}} B \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2\text{O}} C$. Compound $C$ is:
Stephen Reaction.explanation: $\text{CH}_3\text{Br} \xrightarrow{\text{KCN}} \text{CH}_3\text{CN} \xrightarrow{\text{Stephen}} \text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$ (ethanal).

Stephen Reaction.question: Why is stannous chloride a good reducing agent in the Stephen reaction?

options.text: Because tin is an alkali metal
Because $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ readily loses 2 electrons to attain the stable +4 oxidation state ($E^\circ_{\text{Sn}^{4+}/\text{Sn}^{2+}} = +0.15\text{ V}$)
Because tin forms covalent bonds with chlorine

Stephen Reaction.explanation: $\text{Sn}^{2+}$ has a strong thermodynamic driving force to oxidize to the +4 state, donating two electrons to the nitrile group.

Stephen Reaction.question: When 3-nitrobenzonitrile is subjected to Stephen reduction under carefully controlled conditions, the product formed is:
Stephen Reaction.explanation: Under controlled conditions, the cyano group is selectively reduced to an aldehyde without reducing the aromatic nitro group.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the product when cinnamonitrile ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}=\text{CHCN}$) is reduced via Stephen reaction?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: Stephen reduction selectively reduces the cyano group to formyl while preserving the conjugated carbon-carbon double bond.

Stephen Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds gives formaldehyde when subjected to Stephen reaction?

options.text: None, because hydrogen cyanide ($\text{HCN}$) does not yield formaldehyde cleanly via Stephen reduction

Stephen Reaction.explanation: Stephen reduction is not practical for $\text{HCN}$ to make formaldehyde; formaldehyde is not prepared by this route.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the characteristic appearance of the aldimine stannichloride complex precipitate in the reaction flask?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: The complex $[R\text{CH}=\text{NH}_2]_2[\text{SnCl}_6]$ separates as a dense crystalline white solid from the ethereal solution.

Stephen Reaction.question: What happens when an isonitrile ($R-\text{NC}$) is treated with $\text{SnCl}_2 / \text{HCl}$?

options.text: It does NOT give aldehydes via Stephen reaction; it hydrolyzes or reduces differently (secondary amines)

Stephen Reaction.explanation: The Stephen reaction is specific to normal nitriles ($R-\text{CN}$); isonitriles have a different bonding mode and reduce to secondary amines.

Stephen Reaction.question: In the conversion of toluene to benzaldehyde, which sequence uses the Stephen reaction?

options.text: $\text{Toluene} \xrightarrow{\text{Cl}_2 / h\nu} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{Cl} \xrightarrow{\text{KCN}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{CN} \xrightarrow{\text{Stephen}} \text{Phenylacetaldehyde}$ (wait: to make benzaldehyde directly from benzene: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CN} \xrightarrow{\text{Stephen}} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CHO}$)

Stephen Reaction.explanation: Benzonitrile directly yields benzaldehyde upon Stephen reduction.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the effect of water on the first step of the Stephen reaction?

options.text: It hydrolyzes the nitrile prematurely to an amide or carboxylic acid and hydrolyzes $\text{SnCl}_2$
It converts the aldehyde to an ester

Stephen Reaction.explanation: Water prevents precipitation of the aldimine salt and causes side reactions including hydrolysis of the nitrile.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the formal role of $\text{HCl}$ gas passed into the solution during Stephen reduction?

options.text: Bleaches the color of the reaction
Protonates the nitrile nitrogen to increase electrophilicity and forms the insoluble iminium chloride salt

Stephen Reaction.explanation: Protonation of the nitrile ($R-\text{C}\equiv\text{NH}^+$) activates it toward electron acceptance from $\text{Sn}^{2+}$.

Stephen Reaction.question: Which of the following nitriles will react to give hexanal in a Stephen reaction?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: Hexanenitrile has a 6-carbon chain ending in $-\text{CN}$, giving the 6-carbon aldehyde hexanal.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the yield of aldehyde if the aldimine intermediate is treated with $\text{LiAlH}_4$ instead of water?

options.text: Primary amine ($R-\text{CH}_2\text{NH}_2$) is formed instead of aldehyde

Stephen Reaction.explanation: Hydride addition from $\text{LiAlH}_4$ to the imine double bond reduces it to a primary amine.

Stephen Reaction.question: In which exam year did the question 'Which reagent reduces nitriles to aldehydes: $\text{SnCl}_2/\text{HCl}$ or $\text{Zn/HCl}$?' appear in JEE Main?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: The Stephen reaction and its reagent comparison with DIBAL-H is an established frequent question in JEE Main (2019, 2021, 2023).

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the hybridization change of the nitrile carbon during the Stephen reaction (nitrile $\rightarrow$ aldimine $\rightarrow$ aldehyde)?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: Nitrile carbon is $\text{sp}$ hybridized. In aldimine ($>\text{C}=\text{NH}$) and aldehyde ($-\text{CHO}$), the carbon is $\text{sp}^2$ hybridized.

Stephen Reaction.question: Can ketones be prepared by the classic Stephen reduction?

options.text: Yes, ketones are the major product
No, because the starting material is a nitrile which possesses a terminal $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ yielding an aldehyde upon reduction and hydrolysis

Stephen Reaction.explanation: Stephen reduction of nitriles yields aldimines with a hydrogen attached to the imine carbon, yielding aldehydes exclusively upon hydrolysis.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the product when 4-chlorobenzonitrile is treated with $\text{SnCl}_2 / \text{HCl}$ followed by warm water?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: The cyano group is selectively reduced to formyl without displacing the aryl chloride, giving 4-chlorobenzaldehyde.

Stephen Reaction.question: Why is warm water rather than cold water used for the hydrolysis of the aldimine hydrochloride?

options.text: Cold water freezes the aldimine permanently
Warm water accelerates the nucleophilic attack of water on the iminium carbon and drives the equilibrium toward the aldehyde
Warm water oxidizes the aldehyde to acid
Warm water dissolves the ether solvent

Stephen Reaction.explanation: Warming accelerates the hydrolysis rate and assists in the expulsion of the ammonium salt into the aqueous layer.

Stephen Reaction.question: Which of the following statements about the Stephen reaction is CORRECT?

options.text: It reduces a nitrile to an aldehyde with one less carbon atom
It reduces an aldehyde to an alcohol
It converts an alkyl or aryl nitrile into an aldehyde having the SAME number of carbon atoms
It oxidizes an alcohol to a nitrile

Stephen Reaction.explanation: The carbon count is conserved: the nitrile carbon directly becomes the carbonyl carbon of the aldehyde.

Stephen Reaction.question: What is the product of Stephen reduction of 2-naphthonitrile?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: The 2-cyano group is converted to a 2-formyl group, yielding 2-naphthaldehyde.

Stephen Reaction.question: In a classic multi-step synthesis: Benzene $\xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2 / \text{FeBr}_3} A \xrightarrow{\text{CuCN / pyridine, } \Delta} B \xrightarrow{\text{SnCl}_2 / \text{HCl, } \text{H}_2\text{O}} C$. What is $C$?
Stephen Reaction.explanation: Bromobenzene ($A$) undergoes Rosenmund-von Braun reaction with $\text{CuCN}$ to give benzonitrile ($B$), which undergoes Stephen reduction to give benzaldehyde ($C$).

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What are the reagents used in the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction?

options.text: Carboxylic acid with chlorine ($\text{Cl}_2$) or bromine ($\text{Br}_2$) in the presence of a catalytic amount of red phosphorus ($\text{P}_{\text{red}}$), followed by water hydrolysis
Carboxylic acid with thionyl chloride only
Carboxylic acid with nitric acid and sulfuric acid

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: The HVZ reaction selectively halogenates the $\alpha$-position of aliphatic carboxylic acids using halogen ($\text{Br}_2$ or $\text{Cl}_2$) and catalytic red phosphorus.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the major product of the HVZ reaction of acetic acid with bromine and red phosphorus?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Bromination occurs exclusively at the $\alpha$-carbon of acetic acid to yield $\alpha$-bromoacetic acid (bromoacetic acid).

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: Which essential structural feature MUST a carboxylic acid possess to undergo the HVZ reaction?

options.text: At least one $\alpha$-hydrogen atom on the carbon adjacent to the carboxyl group

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: The reaction mechanism proceeds via an enol intermediate involving the $\alpha$-carbon; without an $\alpha$-hydrogen, enolization cannot occur and the reaction fails.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: Which of the following carboxylic acids CANNOT undergo the Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky reaction?

options.text: Trimethylacetic acid (Pivalic acid, $(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-COOH}$) and Benzoic acid

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Pivalic acid ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-COOH}$) and benzoic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COOH}$) have no $\alpha$-hydrogens and cannot undergo $\alpha$-halogenation.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the catalytic role of red phosphorus in the HVZ reaction?

options.text: It reacts in situ with halogen to form phosphorus trihalide ($\text{PBr}_3$ or $\text{PCl}_3$), which converts a portion of the acid into the more easily enolizable acyl halide
It acts as a reducing agent to remove oxygen
It absorbs water to dry the solvent

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Free carboxylic acids enolize very poorly. $\text{PBr}_3$ converts the acid into acyl bromide ($R\text{CH}_2\text{COBr}$), which enolizes rapidly into an enol that reacts with bromine.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the reactive enol intermediate formed during the HVZ bromination of propanoic acid?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Propanoyl bromide tautomerizes to its enol form, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{C(OH)Br}$, whose nucleophilic $\alpha$-carbon attacks molecular bromine.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: How is the $\alpha$-bromo acyl bromide converted to the final $\alpha$-bromo carboxylic acid in the catalytic cycle?

options.text: By exchange with an unreacted molecule of carboxylic acid ($R\text{CH(Br)COBr} + R\text{CH}_2\text{COOH} \rightleftharpoons R\text{CH(Br)COOH} + R\text{CH}_2\text{COBr}$) or by aqueous work-up

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: The $\alpha$-halo acyl bromide undergoes exchange with another molecule of carboxylic acid, regenerating the acyl bromide catalyst and liberating the $\alpha$-halo acid.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: Why cannot iodine or fluorine be used effectively in the standard HVZ reaction?

options.text: Because iodine is an acid and fluorine is a base
Fluorine reacts violently and uncontrollably causing extensive decomposition, while iodination is thermodynamically unfavorable and reversible

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Fluorination is excessively exothermic and non-selective; iodination is endothermic with unfavorable equilibrium. Only chlorine and bromine work well.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the product when propanoic acid is treated with excess bromine and red phosphorus?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: With excess halogen and prolonged reaction times, both $\alpha$-hydrogens on the methylene carbon are sequentially replaced, yielding 2,2-dibromopropanoic acid.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What synthetic transformation occurs when an $\alpha$-bromo carboxylic acid is treated with excess aqueous ammonia?

options.text: Reduction back to the carboxylic acid

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Nucleophilic substitution of the $\alpha$-bromine by ammonia yields $\alpha$-amino acids (e.g., converting propanoic acid via 2-bromopropanoic acid to DL-alanine).

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: How can an $\alpha$-halo acid be converted into an $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated carboxylic acid?

options.text: By dehydrohalogenation using alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ or a hindered base (e.g., $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(Br)COOH} \xrightarrow{\text{alc. KOH}} \text{CH}_2=\text{CH-COOH}$)

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Elimination of hydrogen halide ($E2$) from the $\alpha$-halo acid using alcoholic base creates an $\alpha,\beta$-double bond, yielding acrylic or crotonic acids.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the product when an $\alpha$-bromo acid is treated with warm aqueous $\text{KOH}$?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Aqueous $\text{KOH}$ promotes nucleophilic substitution ($S_N2$) of the bromide by hydroxide, yielding $\alpha$-hydroxy carboxylic acids (e.g. lactic acid from 2-bromopropanoic acid).

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the product when phenylacetic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$) is subjected to the HVZ reaction?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: The benzylic $\alpha$-carbon has two acidic hydrogens and undergoes selective halogenation, giving $\alpha$-bromophenylacetic acid.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: Why does formic acid ($\text{HCOOH}$) NOT give the HVZ reaction?

options.text: It is not a carboxylic acid
It has no $\alpha$-carbon atom (the hydrogen is attached directly to the carbonyl carbon)
It is a gas at room temperature

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Formic acid possesses only a formyl hydrogen and lacks an $\alpha$-carbon, making enolization impossible; halogen oxidizes it to $\text{CO}_2$ instead.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the effect of introducing an $\alpha$-halogen atom on the acidity of a carboxylic acid?

options.text: Acidity increases significantly due to the $-I$ (electron-withdrawing inductive) effect of the electronegative halogen

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: The strongly electronegative halogen stabilizes the carboxylate conjugate base via inductive electron withdrawal: bromoacetic acid ($pK_a \approx 2.90$) is much more acidic than acetic acid ($pK_a \approx 4.76$).

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: Arrange the following in increasing order of acid strength: Acetic acid, Fluoroacetic acid, Chloroacetic acid, Bromoacetic acid:
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Higher electronegativity of the $\alpha$-halogen exerts a stronger electron-withdrawing inductive ($-I$) effect, increasing acidity: $\text{F} > \text{Cl} > \text{Br} > \text{H}$.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the product of the reaction: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH} \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2 / \text{P}_{\text{red}}} A \xrightarrow{\text{KCN}} B \xrightarrow{\text{H}_3\text{O}^+} C$?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Bromoacetic acid ($A$) reacts with cyanide to form cyanoacetic acid ($B$), which upon complete hydrolysis yields the dicarboxylic acid malonic acid ($C$).

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: In the HVZ reaction, why is red phosphorus preferred over white phosphorus?

options.text: Red phosphorus is an acid while white phosphorus is a base
Red phosphorus is non-toxic, non-pyrophoric, and safe to handle, whereas white phosphorus is spontaneously flammable in air and highly toxic
White phosphorus does not react with halogens

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Red phosphorus is stable at room temperature and allows controlled in situ generation of phosphorus halides without fire hazards.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What happens when isobutyric acid ($(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{CHCOOH}$) undergoes HVZ bromination?

options.text: No reaction occurs because it is hindered

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Isobutyric acid has one $\alpha$-hydrogen on its tertiary carbon; bromination replaces this hydrogen selectively to give 2-bromo-2-methylpropanoic acid.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: Can a second bromine atom be introduced into isobutyric acid under HVZ conditions?

options.text: No, because the mono-brominated product has no remaining $\alpha$-hydrogens

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Once the single $\alpha$-hydrogen of isobutyric acid is replaced, the resulting $\alpha$-bromo acid cannot enolize, terminating further halogenation.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the product when butanoic acid is treated with $\text{Br}_2 / \text{P}_{\text{red}}$ followed by $\text{H}_2\text{O}$?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: The HVZ reaction is strictly regiospecific for the $\alpha$-carbon, producing 2-bromobutanoic acid exclusively.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: Why does free molecular bromine NOT react directly with acetic acid in the absence of red phosphorus or acyl chloride?

options.text: Because carboxylic acids exist almost entirely in the keto/carboxyl form and have an extremely low, negligible equilibrium concentration of enol
Because acetic acid is a base

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Unlike ketones, carboxylic acids have very low enol content ($K_{enol} < 10^{-12}$) due to resonance donation from the $-\text{OH}$ group; acyl halides enolize much faster.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: Instead of red phosphorus, which of the following reagents can be added in catalytic amounts to initiate the HVZ bromination?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Direct addition of catalytic $\text{PBr}_3$ or $\text{SOCl}_2$ generates the catalytic acyl halide in situ, bypassing the need for elemental phosphorus.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What gas is continuously evolved during the HVZ bromination of carboxylic acids?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Halogenation of the enol generates one mole of hydrogen bromide gas: $\text{RCH}=\text{C(OH)X} + \text{X}_2 \rightarrow \text{RCH(X)COX} + \text{HX}\uparrow$.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the product when 2-bromopropanoic acid is treated with excess ammonia?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Ammonolysis of 2-bromopropanoic acid substitutes the $\alpha$-bromine with an amino group, synthesizing the essential amino acid alanine.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the synthesis sequence to convert acetic acid into glycine using HVZ reaction?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Chlorination of acetic acid gives chloroacetic acid, which on reaction with excess ammonia undergoes nucleophilic substitution to yield glycine.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the IUPAC name of the product obtained when propanoic acid is subjected to HVZ reaction with bromine?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: The bromine attaches at carbon-2 (the $\alpha$-carbon), yielding 2-bromopropanoic acid.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: Why does 2,2-dimethylpropanoic acid NOT react under HVZ conditions?

options.text: All four valencies of the $\alpha$-carbon are bonded to other carbons (three methyl groups), leaving zero $\alpha$-hydrogens

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Pivalic acid ($(\text{CH}_3)_3\text{C-COOH}$) possesses a quaternary $\alpha$-carbon with no $\alpha$-hydrogens, completely preventing enolization.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the stereochemical outcome when a racemic $\alpha$-bromo carboxylic acid is synthesized via HVZ reaction?

options.text: A racemic mixture ($\pm$) of enantiomers is formed because the planar achiral enol intermediate is attacked from either face with equal probability
A single pure optically active enantiomer

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: The enol intermediate is planar ($\,\text{sp}^2$ hybridized at the $\alpha$-carbon); halogen attacks from the top and bottom faces equally, producing a racemate.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What happens when an $\alpha$-bromo acid is heated with zinc metal in ethanol?

options.text: Coupling to form a dicarboxylic acid
Debromination occurs via reduction back to the parent carboxylic acid ($R\text{CH(Br)COOH} \xrightarrow{\text{Zn/H}^+} R\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$)

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Zinc in acid selectively reduces $\alpha$-halogen substituents, replacing the halogen with hydrogen to regenerate the unsubstituted carboxylic acid.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: Which of the following acids will undergo the HVZ reaction most rapidly?

options.text: Phenylacetic acid ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, because the benzylic enol is resonance-stabilized by the aromatic ring)

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Phenylacetic acid enolizes most readily because the resulting enol/enolate is conjugated with the aromatic $\pi$-system.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the product when adipic acid (hexanedioic acid) is treated with 2 equivalents of $\text{Br}_2 / \text{P}_{\text{red}}$ followed by $\text{H}_2\text{O}$?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Each of the two equivalent $\alpha$-carbons adjacent to the two carboxyl groups undergoes bromination, yielding 2,5-dibromohexanedioic acid.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: When 2,5-dibromohexanedioic acid is treated with base, what useful dicarboxylic acid is synthesized via double dehydrohalogenation?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Double elimination ($2 \times E2$) of $\text{HBr}$ from 2,5-dibromohexanedioic acid introduces two conjugated double bonds, yielding trans,trans-muconic acid.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the product when 2-bromobutanoic acid is treated with potassium cyanide ($\text{KCN}$) followed by acid hydrolysis?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Cyanide displaces bromide via $S_N2$ to form 2-cyanobutanoic acid, which hydrolyzes to ethylmalonic acid.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the purpose of adding water at the conclusion of the HVZ reaction?

options.text: To hydrolyze any remaining $\alpha$-halo acyl bromide and phosphorus halides back into carboxylic acids and phosphorous acid

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: The catalytic cycle generates $\alpha$-halo acyl bromide; water hydrolyzes this intermediate into the desired $\alpha$-halo carboxylic acid while destroying $\text{PBr}_3$.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What happens if an alcohol ($R'\text{OH}$) is added instead of water during the workup of an HVZ reaction?

options.text: The alcohol oxidizes to an aldehyde
An $\alpha$-halo ester ($R\text{CH(Br)COOR}'$) is formed directly in high yield

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: The $\alpha$-halo acyl bromide reacts preferentially with the alcohol nucleophile, enabling one-pot synthesis of $\alpha$-halo esters.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the product when propanoic acid is treated with $\text{Br}_2 / \text{P}_{\text{red}}$, followed by ethanol workup?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: The intermediate 2-bromopropanoyl bromide reacts with ethanol to give ethyl 2-bromopropanoate directly.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: In the HVZ reaction, why does halogenation NOT occur at the $\beta$ or $\gamma$ carbons?

options.text: Because enolization involves ONLY the protons on the $\alpha$-carbon directly adjacent to the carbonyl group
Because the catalyst only binds to $\alpha$-carbons

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Enol formation requires deprotonation at the carbon directly $\alpha$ to the carbonyl; carbons further away cannot form conjugated enols and remain unaffected.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the oxidation state of phosphorus in $\text{PBr}_3$?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Phosphorus is bonded to three electronegative bromine atoms ($-1$ each), giving phosphorus an oxidation state of $+3$.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the major inorganic byproduct obtained during the water quenching of an HVZ reaction using $\text{P}_{\text{red}}$?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Hydrolysis of phosphorus tribromide yields phosphorous acid: $\text{PBr}_3 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{H}_3\text{PO}_3 + 3\text{HBr}$.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds will give a positive HVZ reaction?

options.text: Cyclohexanecarboxylic acid (has one $\alpha$-hydrogen at the ring junction)

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Cyclohexanecarboxylic acid has a single $\alpha$-hydrogen on C-1 of the ring, which is replaced by bromine to give 1-bromocyclohexanecarboxylic acid.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the product of: $\text{Cyclohexanecarboxylic acid} \xrightarrow{\text{Br}_2 / \text{P}_{\text{red}}} \xrightarrow{\text{H}_2\text{O}} X$?
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Bromination occurs selectively at the $\alpha$-methine carbon (C-1) of the cyclohexane ring.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: Identify the reagent $Y$ in: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(Br)COOH} \xrightarrow{Y} \text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)COOH}$:
Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: Aqueous hydroxide or moist silver oxide provides nucleophilic substitution of bromide without causing dehydrohalogenation elimination.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the relative rate of bromination of acyl bromide compared to the parent carboxylic acid?

options.text: Both react at the exact same rate
Acyl bromide enolizes and reacts over $10^5$ times faster than the carboxylic acid

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: The electron-withdrawing bromine atom on the carbonyl accelerates enol formation dramatically compared to the electron-donating $-\text{OH}$ group of the carboxylic acid.

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.question: What is the ultimate synthetic significance of the HVZ reaction in organic chemistry?

options.text: It provides an indispensable, regioselective pathway to convert readily available aliphatic carboxylic acids into $\alpha$-amino acids, $\alpha$-hydroxy acids, and $\alpha,\beta$-unsaturated acids
It is used to synthesize long-chain alkanes
It provides a route to aromatic rings from methane
It is used to crack petroleum

Hell-Volhard-Zelinsky (HVZ) Reaction.explanation: The introduction of an $\alpha$-halogen unlocks versatile nucleophilic substitutions and eliminations to synthesize pharmaceuticals, amino acids, and polymer monomers.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What are the standard reagents and conditions used for the Diazotization reaction of aromatic amines?

options.text: Primary aromatic amine treated with nitrous acid (generated in situ from $\text{NaNO}_2$ and dilute $\text{HCl}$) at ice-cold temperatures ($0-5^\circ\text{C}$ / $273-278\text{ K}$)
Secondary aromatic amine treated with nitric acid at $100^\circ\text{C}$
Tertiary amine treated with sodium nitrate and sulfuric acid at room temperature
Nitrobenzene treated with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Diazotization of primary aromatic amines is carried out using sodium nitrite and dilute hydrochloric acid (producing $\text{HNO}_2$) at $0-5^\circ\text{C}$ to avoid thermal decomposition of the diazonium salt.

Diazotization Reaction.question: Why must the diazotization of aniline be carried out at low temperature ($0-5^\circ\text{C}$)?

options.text: Because benzenediazonium chloride is thermally unstable and rapidly hydrolyzes to phenol with evolution of nitrogen gas ($\text{N}_2$) at temperatures above $5^\circ\text{C}$
Because aniline becomes explosive at higher temperatures

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Benzenediazonium cations decompose unimolecularly into phenyl carbocations with loss of nitrogen gas if warmed above $5^\circ\text{C}$, yielding phenol by reaction with water.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the active electrophilic species responsible for nitrosation in diazotization?

options.text: Nitrosonium ion ($^+\text{N=O}$ or nitrous acidium ion, $\text{H}_2\text{O}^+-\text{NO}$)

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: In acidic medium, nitrous acid is protonated to form $\text{H}_2\text{O}^+-\text{NO}$, which loses water to form the highly reactive, electrophilic nitrosonium ion ($^+\text{N=O}$).

Diazotization Reaction.question: Why is nitrous acid ($\text{HNO}_2$) generated in situ rather than stored on a shelf?

options.text: Nitrous acid is too expensive to manufacture
Nitrous acid is a gas that cannot be liquefied
Nitrous acid is inherently unstable and rapidly disproportionates into nitric acid ($\text{HNO}_3$), nitric oxide ($\text{NO}$), and water at room temperature

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Due to its thermal instability ($3\text{HNO}_2 \rightarrow \text{HNO}_3 + 2\text{NO} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$), nitrous acid must be freshly generated by mixing cold aqueous $\text{NaNO}_2$ with dilute acid.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the balanced equation for the diazotization of aniline?
Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Two equivalents of $\text{HCl}$ are required: one to form aniline hydrochloride and sodium chloride/$\text{HNO}_2$, and the second to maintain acidic medium and supply chloride counterion.

Diazotization Reaction.question: Why are arenediazonium salts more stable than alkanediazonium salts?

options.text: Arenediazonium salts are covalent network solids

Arenediazonium salts are resonance-stabilized by delocalization of the positive charge into the aromatic benzene ring, whereas aliphatic diazonium salts lack resonance and lose $\text{N}_2$ instantaneously
Alkanediazonium salts contain triple bonds while arenediazonium salts do not
Alkanediazonium salts are stabilized by hydrogen bonding

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: In arenediazonium ions, the diazonium group is conjugated with the aromatic $\pi$-system, stabilizing the $\text{C-N}$ bond; aliphatic diazonium ions decompose instantaneously even at $-50^\circ\text{C}$ to form carbocations and $\text{N}_2$.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the product when an aliphatic primary amine (e.g., ethylamine) is treated with $\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl}$ at $0-5^\circ\text{C}$?

options.text: A mixture of alcohol, alkene, and alkyl halide with quantitative and brisk evolution of nitrogen gas ($\text{N}_2$)

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Aliphatic diazonium salts are extremely unstable and decompose immediately, giving ethyl carbocation which yields ethanol, ethene, and ethyl chloride with evolution of $\text{N}_2$ gas.

Diazotization Reaction.question: Why is excess mineral acid (at least 2.5 to 3 equivalents of $\text{HCl}$) used in diazotization reactions?

options.text: To dissolve the glass reaction flask
To neutralize the nitrogen gas formed
To increase the freezing point of the mixture
To keep the solution strongly acidic, prevent side reaction (coupling between diazonium ion and unreacted free aniline to form diazoaminobenzene), and suppress disproportionation of $\text{HNO}_2$

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: In insufficient acid, free unprotonated aniline couples with the newly formed diazonium salt, forming a yellow precipitate of diazoaminobenzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{N=N}-\text{NH}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$).

Diazotization Reaction.question: How is excess nitrous acid destroyed at the end of a diazotization reaction before subsequent coupling?

options.text: By adding urea ($\text{H}_2\text{NCONH}_2$) or sulfamic acid ($\text{H}_2\text{NSO}_3\text{H}$)

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Urea reacts rapidly with excess $\text{HNO}_2$ to release harmless nitrogen and carbon dioxide gases: $2\text{HNO}_2 + \text{NH}_2\text{CONH}_2 \rightarrow 2\text{N}_2 + \text{CO}_2 + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$, preventing unwanted oxidation during downstream coupling.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What test paper is used during diazotization to verify that nitrous acid is in slight excess?

options.text: Starch-iodide (KI-starch) paper, which turns blue-black due to iodine liberation

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Nitrous acid oxidizes iodide ions to free iodine: $2\text{HNO}_2 + 2\text{I}^- + 2\text{H}^+ \rightarrow 2\text{NO} + \text{I}_2 + 2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. Free iodine forms a characteristic deep blue-black complex with starch.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the nature of the bonding in benzenediazonium chloride?

options.text: Ionic salt composed of benzenediazonium cations ($[\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{N}^+\equiv\text{N}]$) and chloride anions ($\text{Cl}^-$)

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Benzenediazonium chloride is a crystalline ionic solid containing discrete diazonium cations and chloride anions; it is water-soluble.

Diazotization Reaction.question: Why is benzenediazonium chloride rarely isolated in the dry solid state?

options.text: Because it is an invisible gas
Because it turns into metallic sodium
Dry crystalline diazonium salts are highly sensitive, unstable, and explode violently upon friction, heat, or minor shock

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Due to tremendous shock-sensitivity and explosiveness in the dry state, diazonium salts are almost always prepared and used immediately in aqueous solution without isolation.

Diazotization Reaction.question: Which arenediazonium salt CAN be safely isolated as a dry, stable crystalline solid at room temperature?
Diazotization Reaction.explanation: The tetrafluoroborate salt ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{BF}_4^-$) is water-insoluble, non-hygroscopic, and remarkably stable at room temperature, allowing safe filtration, drying, and storage.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the first mechanistic step when aniline attacks the nitrosonium ion ($^+\text{NO}$)?

options.text: Attack of the benzene ring on oxygen
Nucleophilic attack of the aniline nitrogen lone pair on the nitrogen of $^+\text{NO}$ to form an $N$-nitrosammonium ion

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: The lone pair on the $-\text{NH}_2$ nitrogen nucleophilically attacks the electrophilic nitrosonium nitrogen: $\text{ArNH}_2 + ^+\text{NO} \rightarrow \text{Ar}-\text{NH}_2^+-\text{NO}$.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What intermediate is formed after deprotonation of the $N$-nitrosammonium ion?
Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Loss of a proton from $\text{Ar}-\text{NH}_2^+-\text{NO}$ yields the neutral $N$-nitroso intermediate $\text{Ar}-\text{NH}-\text{N=O}$.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What tautomeric rearrangement does the $N$-nitroso intermediate undergo during diazotization?

options.text:
Prototropic tautomerization to a diazoic acid / diazonium hydroxide ($
\text{Ar}-\text{N=N-OH}$)

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Proton transfer converts the $N$-nitroso compound into its tautomer, diazenol/diazohydroxide: $\text{Ar}-\text{NH}-\text{N=O} \rightleftharpoons \text{Ar}-\text{N=N}-\text{OH}$.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What final dehydration step yields the diazonium cation ($[\text{Ar}-\text{N}\equiv\text{N}]^+$)?

options.text: Protonation of the $-\text{OH}$ group of $\text{Ar}-\text{N=N-OH}$ followed by departure of water ($\text{H}_2\text{O}$)

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Protonation yields $\text{Ar}-\text{N=N}-\text{OH}_2^+$, which rapidly loses $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ as a leaving group to generate the linear diazonium cation $[\text{Ar}-\text{N}^+\equiv\text{N}]$.

Diazotization Reaction.question: How does a secondary aromatic amine (e.g., $N$-methylaniline) react with nitrous acid?

options.text: It undergoes diazotization to form a diazonium salt
It forms a yellow, water-insoluble oily liquid: $N$-methyl-$N$-nitrosoaniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}(\text{CH}_3)\text{NO}$)
It gives phenol and nitrogen gas
It forms an azo dye immediately

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Secondary amines possess only one hydrogen on nitrogen; after forming the $N$-nitroso compound, they lack the second proton needed for tautomerization and dehydration, stopping at the yellow oily $N$-nitrosoamine.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the Liebermann's Nitroso Reaction used to identify?

options.text: Secondary amines (via formation of $N$-nitrosoamines that give a characteristic deep green/blue color with phenol and conc. $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$)

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Treatment of secondary amine nitroso derivatives with phenol and concentrated sulfuric acid produces an intense green or blue color that turns red on dilution with water and deep blue in alkali.

Diazotization Reaction.question: How does a tertiary aromatic amine (e.g., $N,N$-dimethylaniline) react with nitrous acid?

options.text: It forms a yellow diazonium salt
It undergoes electrophilic aromatic substitution at the para position to form $p$-nitroso-$N,N$-dimethylaniline (a green crystalline solid)

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Tertiary aromatic amines have no hydrogens on nitrogen; instead, electrophilic nitrosonium ($^+\text{NO}$) attacks the strongly activated para position of the aromatic ring.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the hybridization and geometry of the two nitrogen atoms in the diazonium group ($-\text{N}_1^+ \equiv \text{N}_2$)?

options.text: Both nitrogen atoms are $\text{sp}$ hybridized, resulting in a strictly linear $\text{C-N-N}$ arrangement

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: The diazonium triple bond requires $\text{sp}$ hybridization for both nitrogens, dictating a linear $180^\circ$ $\text{C-N-N}$ bond angle.

Diazotization Reaction.question: Why is the diazonium group ($-\text{N}_2^+$) regarded as the ultimate leaving group in organic synthesis?

options.text: Because nitrogen is more electronegative than fluorine
Because it departs as dinitrogen gas ($\text{N}_2$), an exceptionally stable molecule possessing a massive bond dissociation energy ($945\text{ kJ/mol}$) and very high positive entropy of departure
Because nitrogen carries a negative charge
Because nitrogen forms hydrogen bonds with water

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: The extrusion of neutral gaseous $\text{N}_2$ provides an enormous thermodynamic and entropic driving force, making the diazonium moiety the most reactive leaving group known in organic chemistry.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the product when benzenediazonium chloride is warmed with water ($>5^\circ\text{C}$ / $\Delta$)?

options.text: Phenol ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH}$), with evolution of $\text{N}_2$ gas and $\text{HCl}$

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Warm water acts as a nucleophile attacking the phenyl carbocation generated upon thermolysis of benzenediazonium cation: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} + \text{N}_2 + \text{HCl}$.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What happens when benzenediazonium chloride is treated with hypophosphorous acid ($\text{H}_3\text{PO}_2$) and water?

options.text: Reduction of the diazonium group to hydrogen, yielding Benzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_6$)

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Hypophosphorous acid is a mild reducing agent that replaces the diazonium group with hydrogen (deamination): $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- + \text{H}_3\text{PO}_2 + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{C}_6\text{H}_6 + \text{N}_2 + \text{H}_3\text{PO}_3 + \text{HCl}$.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What reagent other than $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_2$ can reduce benzenediazonium chloride directly to benzene?
Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Ethanol acts as a hydride donor to reduce benzenediazonium salt to benzene while being oxidized to ethanal: $\text{ArN}_2^+\text{Cl}^- + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{OH} \rightarrow \text{ArH} + \text{N}_2 + \text{CH}_3\text{CHO} + \text{HCl}$.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the product when benzenediazonium chloride is treated with potassium iodide ($\text{KI}$)?

options.text: Iodobenzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{I}$) with evolution of nitrogen gas

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Iodide is sufficiently nucleophilic and easily oxidized; no copper catalyst is required. Simply warming benzenediazonium chloride with aqueous $\text{KI}$ yields iodobenzene quantitatively.

Diazotization Reaction.question: Can direct iodination of benzene be used to prepare iodobenzene cleanly?

options.text: Benzene does not dissolve in iodine
Direct iodination is reversible, slow, and requires strong oxidizing agents ($\text{HNO}_3$ or $\text{HIO}_3$), making the diazonium route (via $\text{KI}$) far superior and convenient

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Electrophilic iodination of benzene with $\text{I}_2$ has an unfavorable equilibrium; diazotization followed by $\text{KI}$ is the preferred laboratory route to aryl iodides.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the reaction called when benzenediazonium fluoroborate is thermally decomposed to yield fluorobenzene?
Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Dry benzenediazonium tetrafluoroborate decomposes upon mild dry heating to yield fluorobenzene, boron trifluoride, and nitrogen: $\text{ArN}_2^+\text{BF}_4^- \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{Ar-F} + \text{BF}_3 + \text{N}_2$.

Diazotization Reaction.question: Why is the Balz-Schiemann reaction preferred over direct fluorination for preparing aryl fluorides?

options.text: Direct fluorination of benzene with elemental fluorine ($\text{F}_2$) is uncontrollably violent, highly exothermic, and causes extensive carbon-carbon bond cleavage
Fluorine does not react with benzene

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: The reaction of elemental $\text{F}_2$ with organic compounds is dangerously explosive; Balz-Schiemann provides a mild, safe, controlled method to insert a single fluorine atom into aromatic rings.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What happens when benzenediazonium chloride is treated with sodium nitrite in the presence of copper powder or cuprous oxide?
Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Warming benzenediazonium fluoroborate with aqueous sodium nitrite in the presence of copper catalyst displaces the diazonium group to yield nitrobenzene.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the synthetic sequence to convert nitrobenzene into 1,3,5-tribromobenzene?

options.text: Direct bromination of nitrobenzene with 3 moles of $\text{Br}_2$

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Aniline strongly directs ortho/para, enabling tribromination; subsequent diazotization and deamination with $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_2$ strips the amine group, leaving symmetric 1,3,5-tribromobenzene.

Diazotization Reaction.question: Why can meta-bromotoluene NOT be easily prepared by direct bromination of toluene?

options.text: The methyl group is strictly ortho/para-directing, directing bromination almost exclusively to 2- and 4-positions

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: To prepare $m$-bromotoluene, $p$-toluidine is acetylated, brominated meta to methyl (ortho to acetamido), deprotected, diazotized, and deaminated with $\text{H}_3\text{PO}_2$.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the product when benzenediazonium chloride is reduced with stannous chloride and concentrated $\text{HCl}$ (or $\text{Na}_2\text{SO}_3$)?
Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Mild reduction of the diazonium group without cleavage of the nitrogen-nitrogen bond gives phenylhydrazine: $\text{ArN}_2^+\text{Cl}^- + 4[\text{H}] \xrightarrow{\text{SnCl}_2/\text{HCl}} \text{ArNH-NH}_2 \cdot \text{HCl}$.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What famous reagent used to identify aldehydes and ketones is prepared from phenylhydrazine derivatives?
Diazotization Reaction.explanation: 2,4-DNP (Brady's reagent), which condenses with carbonyl compounds to yield brightly colored orange/red hydrazone precipitates, is prepared via diazotization chemistry.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the role of sodium chloride in salting out benzenediazonium salts?

options.text: Increases the ionic strength of the aqueous phase, decreasing the solubility of diazonium salts and causing them to precipitate

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Diazonium salts are ionic electrolytes; high salt concentration forces them to crystallize out of aqueous solution.

Diazotization Reaction.question: How does temperature above $10^\circ\text{C}$ affect the diazotization of aniline?

options.text: The reaction speeds up with $100\%$ purity
Aniline evaporates as a white cloud
Extensive decomposition of the diazonium ion into phenol, which subsequently couples with unreacted diazonium salt to produce dark-colored complex tarry azo byproducts

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Phenol produced by hydrolysis reacts with remaining diazonium salt in an uncontrolled azo coupling, producing complex dark resins and tars.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What happens when an aromatic diamine such as $p$-phenylenediamine is treated with 2 equivalents of $\text{NaNO}_2$ and $\text{HCl}$?
Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Both primary aromatic amino groups undergo diazotization to form a bis-diazonium salt, widely utilized in the manufacturing of disazo dyes (e.g., Congo Red).

Diazotization Reaction.question: Why does anthranilic acid undergo internal diazotization to form a zwitterionic diazonium carboxylate?

options.text: Because anthranilic acid has no nitrogen
The carboxylate group ($\text{COO}^-$) acts as the internal counterion to the diazonium group ($-\text{N}_2^+$), producing a neutral inner salt
Because chlorine cannot bind to anthranilic acid

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Anthranilic acid diazotizes to form benzenediazonium-2-carboxylate, a dipolar inner salt which on mild heating extrudes $\text{CO}_2$ and $\text{N}_2$ to generate benzyne.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What reactive intermediate is generated when benzenediazonium-2-carboxylate is heated?

options.text: Benzyne ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_4$, a highly reactive aryne containing a formal triple bond in the ring)

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Simultaneous loss of nitrogen and carbon dioxide from the adjacent positions of the aromatic ring generates benzyne.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the effect of an electron-withdrawing group (such as $-\text{NO}_2$) at the para position on the stability of arenediazonium salts?

options.text: It converts the amine into an alcohol directly
It decreases the electron density at the diazonium carbon, making the diazonium ion a more powerful electrophile for azo coupling, but stabilizes the salt against explosive dry decomposition

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Electron-withdrawing substituents increase the positive electrophilic character of the diazonium nitrogen, making $p$-nitrobenzenediazonium one of the most reactive coupling agents.

Diazotization Reaction.question: Why can ortho-phenylenediamine NOT form a bis-diazonium salt under standard conditions?

options.text: Upon diazotization of one amino group, the adjacent amino group attacks the diazonium nitrogen intramolecularly to form 1,2,3-benzotriazole
Because ortho positions are too crowded for chlorine
Because ortho-phenylenediamine is insoluble in acid

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Intramolecular cyclization occurs with extreme rapidity to yield the stable heterocyclic compound benzotriazole.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the product when sulfanilic acid is diazotized?

options.text: A stable zwitterionic diazonium sulfonate inner salt ($^+\text{N}_2-\text{C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{SO}_3^-$)

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Sulfanilic acid forms an inner diazonium sulfonate zwitterion that precipitates as white crystals and is a key intermediate for the synthesis of methyl orange.

Diazotization Reaction.question: In the synthesis of methyl orange, what are the two coupling partners?

options.text: Diazotized sulfanilic acid and $N,N$-dimethylaniline in slightly acidic medium

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Methyl orange is prepared by coupling diazotized sulfanilic acid with $N,N$-dimethylaniline in the presence of dilute acetic acid.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What happens when benzenediazonium chloride is treated with sodium azide ($\text{NaN}_3$)?

options.text: Phenyl azide ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_3$) is formed with evolution of $\text{N}_2$

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: Azide ion nucleophilically attacks the diazonium terminal nitrogen to give a pentazene intermediate which eliminates $\text{N}_2$, yielding phenyl azide.

Diazotization Reaction.question: What is the total number of nitrogen atoms in the diazonium group ($-\text{N}_2^+$)?

options.text: Two nitrogen atoms sharing a formal triple bond

Diazotization Reaction.explanation: The diazo group comprises two contiguous nitrogen atoms ($-\overset{+}{\text{N}}\equiv\text{N}:$) bonded to the aromatic ring carbon.

Coupling Reaction.question: What type of reaction mechanism does azo coupling represent in organic chemistry?

options.text: Electrophilic Aromatic Substitution ($\text{S}_\text{E}\text{Ar}$), where the diazonium ion acts as a weak electrophile attacking an activated aromatic ring

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Azo coupling is an electrophilic aromatic substitution in which the positively charged diazonium ion $[\text{Ar}-\text{N}\equiv\text{N}]^+$ acts as a relatively weak electrophile attacking strongly activated aromatic rings (phenols, naphthols, or aromatic amines).

Coupling Reaction.question: Why can only strongly activated aromatic rings (like phenols and amines) undergo azo coupling?

options.text: Because benzenediazonium ion is a super-electrophile that destroys unactivated rings
Because the arenediazonium ion ($[\text{Ar}-\text{N}\equiv\text{N}]^+$) is a relatively weak, bulky electrophile due to resonance delocalization of positive charge over both nitrogens
Because diazonium ions only dissolve in liquid phenol

Coupling Reaction.explanation: The electrophilicity of diazonium ions is moderate; unactivated or deactivated benzene rings (e.g., benzene, toluene, chlorobenzene, nitrobenzene) are not electron-rich enough to react with them.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is the optimal pH range for the coupling reaction between benzenediazonium chloride and phenol?
Coupling Reaction.explanation: At $\text{pH } 9-10$, phenol is converted into its phenoxide ion ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{O}^-$), which has a much greater electron-donating effect than neutral phenol, accelerating electrophilic attack by diazonium ion.

Coupling Reaction.question: Why is azo coupling with phenol NOT carried out at strongly alkaline pH ($\text{pH } > 11$)?

options.text: Because the azo dye hydrolyzes instantly
Because sodium hydroxide boils at high pH
At high pH, the diazonium ion is converted into an unreactive covalent diazotate ion ($\text{Ar-N=N-O}^-$), which is non-electrophilic

Coupling Reaction.explanation: In strongly alkaline solution: $\text{Ar-N}_2^+ + 2\text{OH}^- \rightleftharpoons \text{Ar}-\text{N=N-O}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$. The diazotate anion lacks positive charge and cannot act as an electrophile.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is the optimal pH range for the coupling reaction between benzenediazonium chloride and aromatic amines (e.g., aniline)?
Coupling Reaction.explanation: At $\text{pH } 4-5$, sufficient free (unprotonated) amine is present to act as an active nucleophile, while preventing protonation of amine into unreactive anilinium ion and preventing diazotate formation.

Coupling Reaction.question: Why is azo coupling with aniline NOT carried out in strongly acidic medium ($\text{pH } < 3$)?

options.text: The diazonium ion decomposes into phenol
Aniline is protonated into anilinium ion ($-\text{NH}_3^+$), which is strongly deactivating and meta-directing, completely shutting down electrophilic attack
