Coupling Reaction.explanation: The anilinium ion has no lone pair to activate the aromatic ring; thus, coupling cannot proceed in strongly acidic conditions.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is the structure and color of the azo dye obtained by coupling benzenediazonium chloride with phenol?
Coupling Reaction.explanation: Phenol couples predominantly at the para position: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N}_2^+\text{Cl}^- + \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{OH} \xrightarrow{\text{OH}^-, \text{pH } 9-10} p\text{-HO-C}_6\text{H}_4-\text{N=N}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5 + \text{Cl}^- + \text{H}_2\text{O}$ (Orange dye).

Coupling Reaction.question: What is the structure and color of the azo dye formed by coupling benzenediazonium chloride with aniline?
Coupling Reaction.explanation: Coupling of benzenediazonium chloride with aniline in mildly acidic medium ($	ext{pH } 4-5$) produces yellow $p$-aminoazobenzene.

Coupling Reaction.question: Why does azo coupling occur predominantly at the para position relative to the activating group (-\text{OH} or -\text{NH}_2)?

options.text: Because the diazonium cation is a bulky electrophile, steric hindrance disfavors ortho attack, directing substitution almost exclusively to the less hindered para position
Because ortho positions are blocked by chlorine
Because meta positions are more reactive

Coupling Reaction.explanation: The diazonium group is sterically demanding; unless the para position is already blocked, coupling occurs selectively at the open para position.

Coupling Reaction.question: What happens during azo coupling if the para position of the phenol is already occupied (e.g., in $p$-cresol)?

options.text: No reaction occurs under any condition
Coupling takes place at one of the unoccupied ortho positions to the $-\text{OH}$ group
The methyl group is displaced as methane gas
The ring opens to form an aliphatic dialdehyde

Coupling Reaction.explanation: If the para position is blocked by a substituent, electrophilic attack by the diazonium ion is directed to the ortho position relative to the activating $-\text{OH}$ group.

Coupling Reaction.question: Why are azo compounds intensely colored and widely used as commercial dyes?

options.text: Because nitrogen atoms emit fluorescent radiation
Because of impurities in the glassware

They possess an extended conjugated system of alternating double and single bonds spanning two aromatic rings connected by the azo chromophore ($-\text{N=N}-$), which absorbs light in the visible spectrum
Because of high molecular weight alone

Coupling Reaction.explanation: The azo group ($-\text{N=N}-$) serves as an excellent chromophore. Delocalization across both aromatic rings narrows the $\text{HOMO-LUMO}$ energy gap, shifting absorption into the visible spectrum.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is the product when benzenediazonium chloride is coupled with $\beta$-naphthol (2-naphthol) in alkaline solution?
Coupling Reaction.explanation: $\beta$-Naphthol couples exclusively at the 1-position (ortho to the 2-hydroxy group) because attack at C1 preserves the aromaticity of the other benzene ring in the Wheland intermediate.

Coupling Reaction.question: Why does $\beta$-naphthol couple exclusively at the 1-position and NEVER at the 3-position?

options.text: Attack at the 1-position yields a resonance-stabilized arenium ion that preserves the intact benzene sextet, whereas attack at the 3-position disrupts aromatic resonance throughout the entire bicyclic system
The 3-position is blocked by a proton that cannot be removed
The 3-position has a formal positive charge

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Electrophilic attack at C1 produces 2 favorable resonance contributors with an intact benzene ring, whereas attack at C3 produces none without disrupting the second ring.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is the name of the qualitative analytical test based on $\beta$-naphthol coupling used to confirm primary aromatic amines?
Coupling Reaction.explanation: The amine is diazotized with $\text{NaNO}_2 + \text{HCl}$ at $0-5^\circ\text{C}$ and poured into an alkaline solution of $\beta$-naphthol; formation of a brilliant scarlet-red dye confirms a primary aromatic amine.

Coupling Reaction.question: Can aliphatic primary amines give a positive Azo Dye Test with $\beta$-naphthol?

options.text: No, because aliphatic diazonium ions decompose instantaneously with loss of $\text{N}_2$ gas and never survive to couple with $\beta$-naphthol

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Aliphatic diazonium ions are exceedingly unstable; they lose dinitrogen within picoseconds to form carbocations, yielding alcohols and alkenes instead of azo dyes.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is the starting material and second component for the preparation of the acid-base indicator Methyl Orange?
Coupling Reaction.explanation: Diazotized sulfanilic acid is coupled with $N,N$-dimethylaniline in mildly acidic aqueous solution to yield methyl orange dye.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is the color change of Methyl Orange across its transition pH range ($3.1 - 4.4$)?

options.text: Red in acidic medium ($\text{pH } < 3.1$) to Yellow in alkaline/neutral medium ($\text{pH } > 4.4$)
Yellow in acidic to Blue in basic
Colorless in acidic to Pink in basic
Green in acidic to Orange in basic

Coupling Reaction.explanation: In acidic solution, protonation occurs at the azo nitrogen, forming a quinonoid resonance contributor with a narrower $\text{HOMO-LUMO}$ gap that absorbs green light and appears red.

Coupling Reaction.question: Why does Methyl Orange turn red upon protonation in acidic solution?

options.text: Protonation at the azo nitrogen forms a highly delocalized quinonoid structure extending across both rings, shifting the absorption spectrum bathochromically (to longer wavelengths)
Because the molecule cleaves into two halves
Because methyl groups dissociate into methane

Coupling Reaction.explanation: The quinonoid form has extensive resonance delocalization between the terminal dimethylamino group and the sulfonic acid moiety, shifting absorption from blue to green (appearing red).

Coupling Reaction.question: What is the structure of Congo Red, a classic direct dye for cotton?

options.text: A disazo dye formed by coupling tetrazotized benzidine with two molecules of naphthionic acid (4-amino-1-naphthalenesulfonic acid)

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Congo Red contains two azo linkages ($-\text{N=N}-$) linking a central biphenyl core to two 1-amino-4-sulfonaphthalene end-groups.

Coupling Reaction.question: What happens during azo coupling when an electron-withdrawing group (such as $-\text{NO}_2$) is present on the arenediazonium ion?

options.text: The coupling reaction is completely inhibited
The diazonium ion turns into a nucleophile
The reaction requires a temperature above $200^\circ\text{C}$
The coupling reaction proceeds significantly faster because the electron-withdrawing group increases the positive charge density and electrophilicity of the diazonium group

Coupling Reaction.explanation: $p$-Nitrobenzenediazonium ion is a substantially more potent electrophile than unsubstituted benzenediazonium ion and can even couple with reactive ethers (e.g., anisole).

Coupling Reaction.question: Which of the following diazonium ions is the most reactive electrophile in azo coupling?
Coupling Reaction.explanation: Strongly electron-withdrawing nitro groups at the 2, 4, and 6 positions maximally deplete electron density from the diazonium group, rendering it a ferocious electrophile.

Coupling Reaction.question: Which of the following aromatic substrates is LEAST likely to undergo azo coupling with benzenediazonium chloride?
Coupling Reaction.explanation: Nitrobenzene is strongly deactivated by the $-\text{NO}_2$ group; weak electrophiles like diazonium ions can only substitute strongly activated rings (phenols, amines).

Coupling Reaction.question: When aniline is treated with benzenediazonium chloride at $\text{pH } 7$, what intermediate is preferentially formed initially before rearrangement?

options.text: Diazoaminobenzene ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5-\text{N=N}-\text{NH}-\text{C}_6\text{H}_5$), where coupling occurred at nitrogen rather than carbon

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Under neutral conditions, the diazonium electrophile attacks the amino nitrogen lone pair (kinetic control) to yield the yellow crystalline diazoaminobenzene.

Coupling Reaction.question: How is diazoaminobenzene rearranged into the thermodynamically stable $C$-coupled product ($p$-aminoazobenzene)?

options.text: By adding excess sodium hydroxide at $0^\circ\text{C}$
By heating with aniline hydrochloride at $40-50^\circ\text{C}$ in the presence of acid

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Acid protonates diazoaminobenzene, which cleaves reversibly back into diazonium ion and aniline; the diazonium ion then attacks the para carbon of aniline irreversibly.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is an auxochrome in an azo dye molecule?

options.text: A functional group ($-\text{OH}$, $-\text{NH}_2$, $-\text{NR}_2$, $-\text{SO}_3\text{Na}$) that deepens the color and binds or fastens the dye to fabric fibers
The group that bleaches the dye

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Auxochromes contain non-bonding lone pairs that conjugate with the $\pi$-system, shifting absorption bathochromically and conferring water solubility or fabric affinity.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is a chromophore in an azo dye?

options.text: The light-absorbing unsaturated group containing $\pi$-electrons, specifically the azo linkage ($-\text{N=N}-$)

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Chromophores (such as $-\text{N=N}-$, $-\text{NO}_2$, $-\text{C=O}$) are structural entities responsible for selective absorption of visible light.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is the product when resorcinol (benzene-1,3-diol) is coupled with benzenediazonium chloride?

options.text: Sudan Orange G (4-(phenyldiazenyl)benzene-1,3-diol), where substitution occurs at C4 (ortho to one -OH, para to the other)

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Both hydroxyl groups reinforce activation at the 4-position (which is ortho to C3 and para to C1); C2 is heavily sterically hindered by both adjacent hydroxyls.

Coupling Reaction.question: Why is coupling at position 2 of resorcinol disfavored compared to position 4?

options.text: Position 2 is sterically crowded between two bulky hydroxyl groups, whereas position 4 is much less hindered

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Steric hindrance between the two neighboring $-\text{OH}$ substituents prevents attack of the bulky diazonium ion at C2, directing it to position 4.

Coupling Reaction.question: What happens when an azo dye is treated with strong reducing agents such as $\text{SnCl}_2 + \text{HCl}$ or $\text{Na}_2\text{S}_2\text{O}_4$?

options.text: Reductive cleavage of the azo bond ($-\text{N=N}-$) occurs, yielding two molecules of primary aromatic amines

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Reductive cleavage: $\text{Ar}-\text{N=N}-\text{Ar}' + 4[\text{H}] \rightarrow \text{Ar}-\text{NH}_2 + \text{Ar}'-\text{NH}_2$. This reaction is historically used to identify the structure of azo dyes.

Coupling Reaction.question: When $p$-aminoazobenzene is reduced with tin and concentrated hydrochloric acid, what are the products?
Coupling Reaction.explanation: Cleavage of the central azo bond delivers one molecule of aniline and one molecule of benzene-1,4-diamine ($p$-phenylenediamine).

Coupling Reaction.question: Why is butter yellow ($p$-dimethylaminoazobenzene), formerly used to color butter, banned as a food additive?

options.text: It is a potent liver carcinogen that causes hepatic tumors in animal models upon metabolic azo reduction and bioactivation

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Azo reduction of butter yellow generates reactive carcinogenic aromatic amine metabolites; it is strictly prohibited worldwide.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is Prontosil, the first commercially available synthetic antibacterial drug discovered by Gerhard Domagk?

options.text: A red azo dye containing a sulfonamide group, which is metabolically cleaved in vivo into the active antibacterial agent sulfanilamide

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Prontosil is a prodrug; in the mammalian body, azoreductase enzymes reduce its azo linkage to release free sulfanilamide, which inhibits bacterial folic acid synthesis.

Coupling Reaction.question: In which medium does $\alpha$-naphthol (1-naphthol) undergo azo coupling with benzenediazonium ion?

options.text: Predominantly at the 4-position in alkaline solution

Coupling Reaction.explanation: $\alpha$-Naphthol couples mainly at position 4 (para to $-\text{OH}$); if position 4 is blocked, coupling takes place at position 2.

Coupling Reaction.question: What type of isomerism is exhibited by azo compounds containing the $-\text{N=N}-$ linkage?
Coupling Reaction.explanation: Due to restricted rotation about the nitrogen-nitrogen double bond, azo compounds exist as trans (E) and cis (Z) isomers; the trans isomer is thermodynamically much more stable.

Coupling Reaction.question: What happens when trans-azobenzene is exposed to ultraviolet light ($\text{UV}$)?

options.text: It breaks into two molecules of benzene
It undergoes reversible photoisomerization to cis-azobenzene, changing its absorption spectrum and dipole moment

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Azobenzene is a prototypical molecular photoswitch: $\text{UV}$ light drives trans-to-cis isomerization, while visible light or heat reverses it back to trans.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is the geometry around each nitrogen atom in trans-azobenzene ($\text{Ph-N=N-Ph}$)?

options.text: Bent with approximately $120^\circ$ bond angles ($\text{sp}^2$ hybridized)

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Each nitrogen in the $-\text{N=N}-$ group is $\text{sp}^2$ hybridized, having one single bond to carbon, one double bond to nitrogen, and one lone pair, yielding a bent geometry.

Coupling Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds CANNOT undergo azo coupling with benzenediazonium chloride?
Coupling Reaction.explanation: Toluene contains only a weakly activating alkyl group ($+I$, hyperconjugation), which is insufficient to activate the ring for attack by the weak diazonium electrophile.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is the effect of an electron-donating substituent (such as $-\text{OCH}_3$) on the diazonium ion during coupling?

options.text: It speeds up coupling by $1000$ times
It decreases the positive charge on the diazonium nitrogen, drastically lowering its electrophilicity and slowing down the coupling reaction
It converts the diazonium salt into an alkane
It makes coupling independent of pH

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Electron donation stabilizes the diazonium cation through resonance, diminishing its electrophilic character and reactivity toward coupling substrates.

Coupling Reaction.question: Why is the reaction temperature strictly maintained at $0-5^\circ\text{C}$ during azo coupling?

options.text: To keep the azo dye in liquid state
To prevent freezing of the water
To prevent thermal hydrolysis of the arenediazonium salt into phenol and evolution of nitrogen gas
To maximize the speed of light absorption

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Diazonium ions hydrolyze rapidly at temperatures above $5-10^\circ\text{C}$; maintaining an ice-cold temperature ensures that the diazonium ion remains intact to couple cleanly.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is the role of sodium acetate in azo coupling with amines?

options.text: It serves as the main oxidizing agent
It bleaches the color of the dye
It acts as a buffer to maintain the $\text{pH}$ around $4-5$, neutralizing the $\text{HCl}$ liberated during the reaction without making the solution strongly basic

Coupling Reaction.explanation: As coupling proceeds, $\text{HCl}$ is generated: $\text{ArN}_2^+\text{Cl}^- + \text{Ar}'\text{NH}_2 \rightarrow \text{Ar}-\text{N=N}-\text{Ar}'\text{NH}_2 + \text{HCl}$. Sodium acetate buffers the reaction so acidity does not rise to the point of deactivating the amine.

Coupling Reaction.question: Why does azo coupling of benzenediazonium ion with pyrrole occur readily without a catalyst?

options.text: Pyrrole is an exceedingly electron-rich, $\pi$-excessive heteroaromatic ring that reacts readily even with weak electrophiles
Pyrrole contains a strong mineral acid

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Pyrrole possesses 6 $\pi$-electrons distributed over only 5 ring atoms, giving it very high electron density; it couples smoothly with diazonium ions at position 2.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is Tartrazine (FD&C Yellow 5), widely used in foods and cosmetics?

options.text: A synthetic yellow azo dye containing pyrazole and sulfonate rings

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Tartrazine is a water-soluble pyrazolone azo dye synthesized via azo coupling chemistry, commonly added to candies, soft drinks, and seasonings.

Coupling Reaction.question: What test distinguishes 1-naphthol from 2-naphthol using diazotized sulfanilic acid?

options.text: 1-Naphthol couples at the 4-position giving a reddish-brown dye, whereas 2-naphthol couples at the 1-position giving a bright red/scarlet crystalline dye with different chromatographic mobility

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Both undergo coupling at different positions (C4 vs C1), producing distinct azo dyes with different shades, melting points, and spectral characteristics.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is the intermediate formed during the electrophilic attack of benzenediazonium ion on phenoxide ion?

options.text: A resonance-stabilized $\sigma$-complex (Wheland intermediate) containing a cyclohexadienone core before losing a proton

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Electrophilic attack by $[\text{Ar}-\text{N}_2]^+$ at the para position of phenoxide forms a cyclohexadienone $\sigma$-complex that rapidly loses a proton to re-aromatize into the azo phenoxide.

Coupling Reaction.question: What is the overall reaction classification for azo coupling in dyes manufacturing?

options.text: Carbon-nitrogen bond-forming electrophilic aromatic substitution reaction

Coupling Reaction.explanation: Azo coupling creates a new $\text{C-N}$ covalent bond between an aromatic ring carbon of the nucleophilic substrate and the terminal nitrogen of the diazonium cation.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What are the reagents and conditions used in the Carbylamine Reaction?

options.text: Primary amine with chloroform ($\text{CHCl}_3$) and alcoholic potassium hydroxide ($\text{KOH}$), warmed gently
Secondary amine with carbon tetrachloride and sodium hydroxide
Tertiary amine with chloroform and sulfuric acid
Amide with bromine and aqueous potassium hydroxide

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: The carbylamine reaction involves heating a primary aliphatic or aromatic amine with chloroform and alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ to form an intensely foul-smelling isocyanide (carbylamine).

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the characteristic observation of the Carbylamine reaction?

options.text: Formation of an extremely offensive, foul, nauseating smell due to the production of an isocyanide (carbylamine, $R-\text{N}\equiv\text{C}$)
Precipitation of a bright yellow canary solid
Effervescence of colorless, odorless hydrogen gas

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Isocyanides (carbylamines) possess a uniquely obnoxious, penetrating, foul odor detectable even in trace quantities, serving as a diagnostic qualitative test.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: Which class of compounds gives a positive Carbylamine test?

options.text: Primary ($1^\circ$) aliphatic and aromatic amines only

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: The carbylamine test is exclusively given by primary amines ($R-\text{NH}_2$ and $\text{Ar}-\text{NH}_2$). Secondary and tertiary amines do not have the required two acidic protons on nitrogen to undergo elimination to isocyanides.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the electrophilic reactive intermediate generated in the Carbylamine reaction?
Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Strong base ($\text{OH}^-$) deprotonates chloroform to form the trichloromethyl carbanion ($^-\text{CCl}_3$), which rapidly eliminates chloride ion via $\alpha$-elimination to generate neutral, electron-deficient singlet dichlorocarbene ($:\text{CCl}_2$).

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What type of elimination leads to the formation of dichlorocarbene from chloroform?
Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Both the proton and the chloride leaving group are removed from the exact same carbon atom (C-1), which is defined as an $\alpha$-elimination (or 1,1-elimination).

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the balanced equation for the carbylamine reaction of ethylamine?
Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Three moles of base are required: one mole to generate dichlorocarbene and two moles to deprotonate the ammonium intermediate, yielding ethyl isocyanide, 3 KCl, and 3 $\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: Does aniline ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NH}_2$) give a positive Carbylamine test?

options.text: No, because the nitrogen lone pair is involved in resonance with the benzene ring
No, because aromatic amines are acidic
Yes, aniline is a primary aromatic amine and reacts to produce phenyl isocyanide (phenyl carbylamine, $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{NC}$) with an offensive odor

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Both aliphatic and aromatic primary amines have two hydrogens on nitrogen and undergo the reaction; aniline yields phenyl isocyanide.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: Which of the following amines will NOT give the Carbylamine test?
Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Dimethylamine is a $2^\circ$ amine and trimethylamine is a $3^\circ$ amine. Neither has two protons on nitrogen, so neither can form an isocyanide.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: Why do secondary amines ($R_2\text{NH}$) fail to give the carbylamine reaction?

options.text: Because secondary amines possess only one hydrogen on nitrogen, preventing the second dehydrohalogenation needed to form the isocyanide triple bond
Because secondary amines are too basic
Because secondary amines oxidize immediately to nitro compounds
Because secondary amines do not react with dichlorocarbene

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: After nucleophilic attack on dichlorocarbene and initial elimination of one $\text{HCl}$, the intermediate $R_2\text{N}^+=\text{CH-Cl}$ has no second proton on nitrogen for further elimination to form $R-\text{N}\equiv\text{C}$.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the nature of the chemical bonding in an isocyanide ($R-\text{N}\equiv\text{C}$)?

options.text: A formal triple bond between nitrogen and carbon consisting of two covalent bonds and one coordinate covalent (dative) bond from nitrogen to carbon: $R-\text{N}^+\equiv\text{C}^-$

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: The isocyanide functional group is represented by the dipolar resonance structure $R-\overset{+}{\text{N}}\equiv\overset{-}{\text{C}}$, where nitrogen donates a lone pair into carbon's empty orbital.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: How can the obnoxious smell of isocyanides be safely destroyed after performing the carbylamine test?

options.text: By adding concentrated hydrochloric acid ($\text{HCl}$), which rapidly hydrolyzes the isocyanide into an odorless primary amine salt and formic acid

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Acid-catalyzed hydrolysis of isocyanide is extremely fast: $R-\text{NC} + 2\text{H}_2\text{O} + \text{HCl} \rightarrow R-\text{NH}_3^+\text{Cl}^- + \text{HCOOH}$, instantaneously neutralizing the stench.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the product when an isocyanide is hydrolyzed in dilute acid?

options.text: A primary amine and formic acid ($R-\text{NH}_2 + \text{HCOOH}$)

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Unlike nitriles ($R-\text{CN}$) which hydrolyze to give carboxylic acids with the same number of carbons, isocyanides ($R-\text{NC}$) cleave the $\text{C-N}$ bond to give a primary amine ($R-\text{NH}_2$) and formic acid ($\text{HCOOH}$).

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the product when an isocyanide is reduced by catalytic hydrogenation ($\text{H}_2/\text{Ni}$) or $\text{LiAlH}_4$?

options.text: A secondary amine containing a methyl group ($R-\text{NH}-\text{CH}_3$)

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Reduction adds four hydrogen atoms across the isocyanide group: $R-\text{N}\equiv\text{C} + 4[\text{H}] \rightarrow R-\text{NH}-\text{CH}_3$, cleanly producing an $N$-methyl secondary amine.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: Which of the following reagents can distinguish between ethylamine and diethylamine?
Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Ethylamine ($1^\circ$) produces an intensely foul-smelling isocyanide, while diethylamine ($2^\circ$) does not react under carbylamine conditions.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the role of alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ rather than aqueous $\text{KOH}$ in the carbylamine reaction?

options.text: Alcoholic $\text{KOH}$ acts as a solvent only
Aqueous $\text{KOH}$ converts chloroform to phosgene immediately
Alcoholic medium provides better solubility for organic reactants (chloroform and amine) and provides higher basicity to promote $\alpha$-elimination

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Chloroform and amines are poorly soluble in water; alcohol acts as a mutual solvent and accelerates the deprotonation of chloroform into dichlorocarbene.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: Can carbon tetrachloride ($\text{CCl}_4$) be used instead of chloroform in the carbylamine reaction?

options.text: Yes, but it requires zinc dust
Yes, it gives an odorless product
No, because $\text{CCl}_4$ has no hydrogen atom to be abstracted by base and cannot generate dichlorocarbene via base deprotonation

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Generating dichlorocarbene requires the abstraction of a proton by base followed by loss of chloride; $\text{CCl}_4$ lacks a hydrogen atom and is completely unreactive.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: Can bromoform ($\text{CHBr}_3$) or iodoform ($\text{CHI}_3$) give the carbylamine reaction with primary amines?

options.text: Yes, they generate dibromocarbene ($:\text{CBr}_2$) or diiodocarbene ($:\text{CI}_2$) and yield the corresponding isocyanides
No, because bromine is too heavy

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: All haloforms possessing a CH bond with halogens undergo $\alpha$-elimination with base to form dihalocarbenes and give the carbylamine test.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: In the mechanism of carbylamine reaction, what acts as the nucleophile that attacks dichlorocarbene?

options.text: The lone pair of electrons on the nitrogen atom of the primary amine

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Dichlorocarbene has a sextet of electrons and an empty p-orbital; the electron-rich nitrogen lone pair of the primary amine acts as a nucleophile, attacking the carbene carbon.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the formal charge on the carbon atom in an isocyanide molecule ($R-\text{N}\equiv\text{C}$)?
Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: The carbon atom has one lone pair (2 electrons) and shares three bonding pairs with nitrogen (3 electrons), giving 5 valence electrons compared to 4 in neutral carbon: formal charge = $4 - (2 + 3) = -1$.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the formal charge on the nitrogen atom in an isocyanide molecule ($R-\text{N}\equiv\text{C}$)?
Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Nitrogen forms four covalent bonds (one single bond to $R$ and a triple bond to carbon) with no lone pairs: formal charge = $5 - (0 + 4) = +1$.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the geometry around the nitrogen atom in methyl isocyanide ($\text{CH}_3-\text{N}\equiv\text{C}$)?
Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: The nitrogen atom is $\text{sp}$ hybridized and participates in a triple bond with carbon and a single bond with $R$, giving a linear geometry.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds will give a positive carbylamine test?
Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Benzylamine is a primary amine ($-\text{NH}_2$) and gives a positive carbylamine test. $N$-methylaniline is $2^\circ$, $N,N$-dimethylaniline is $3^\circ$, and acetamide is an amide (not an amine).

Carbylamine Reaction.question: Why do amides (like $\text{CH}_3\text{CONH}_2$) NOT give the carbylamine test despite having a $-\text{NH}_2$ group?

options.text: Because amides are insoluble in chloroform
Because the lone pair on nitrogen is strongly delocalized into the carbonyl group by resonance, rendering the nitrogen non-nucleophilic toward dichlorocarbene

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Amide nitrogens have very low nucleophilicity due to resonance delocalization ($-\overset{..}{\text{N}}\text{H}_2 \leftrightarrow =\overset{+}{\text{N}}\text{H}_2$), preventing attack on dichlorocarbene.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What happens when phenyl isocyanide is heated with sulfur powder?

options.text: Benzene and carbon disulfide are formed

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Isocyanides have a nucleophilic divalent carbon that readily adds sulfur to form isothiocyanates: $R-\text{NC} + \text{S} \xrightarrow{\Delta} R-\text{N=C=S}$.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What happens when phenyl isocyanide is treated with mercuric oxide ($\text{HgO}$)?

options.text: Phenyl isocyanate ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{N=C=O}$) is formed along with metallic mercury

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Mercuric oxide oxidizes the terminal divalent carbon of isocyanide to isocyanate: $R-\text{NC} + \text{HgO} \rightarrow R-\text{N=C=O} + \text{Hg}$.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the dipole moment of methyl isocyanide compared to methyl cyanide?

options.text: Methyl isocyanide is completely nonpolar ($0\text{ D}$)
Methyl isocyanide has a high dipole moment ($\approx 3.8\text{ D}$) due to permanent formal charges on nitrogen ($+1$) and carbon ($-1$)
Methyl isocyanide has a negative dipole moment
Methyl cyanide has no dipole moment

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Due to the dipolar ionic structure $\text{CH}_3-\overset{+}{\text{N}}\equiv\overset{-}{\text{C}}$, isocyanides possess large dipole moments.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the boiling point of an alkyl isocyanide compared to its isomeric alkyl cyanide?

options.text: Isocyanides boil much higher than nitriles
Isocyanides have significantly lower boiling points than their isomeric nitriles (cyanides) due to less efficient intermolecular association

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Methyl isocyanide boils at $59.6^\circ\text{C}$, whereas acetonitrile (methyl cyanide) boils at $81.6^\circ\text{C}$. Nitriles form stronger dipole-dipole alignments than isocyanides.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the product when methylamine is reacted with $\text{CHCl}_3$ and alcoholic $\text{KOH}$?
Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Reaction of methylamine with chloroform and base produces methyl isocyanide (methyl carbylamine), an extremely pungent compound.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: Why is the carbylamine test considered extremely sensitive?

options.text: The human olfactory system can detect the intolerable stench of isocyanides at concentrations as low as parts per billion (ppb)
It changes color from red to blue at $1\mu\text{M}$

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Isocyanides have an astonishingly low odor threshold, making the test extraordinarily sensitive for detecting trace primary amines.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: Which of the following isomers of $\text{C}_3\text{H}_9\text{N}$ will give a positive carbylamine test?

options.text: Propan-1-amine and Propan-2-amine (both are primary amines)

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Only the primary amine isomers (1-propanamine and 2-propanamine) give the carbylamine test. Secondary ($N$-methylethanamine) and tertiary (trimethylamine) isomers do not.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the intermediate formed immediately after the attack of $R\text{NH}_2$ on dichlorocarbene?
Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Nucleophilic addition of neutral amine to neutral carbene produces the zwitterion $R-\text{NH}_2^+-\bar{\text{C}}\text{Cl}_2$ containing positive nitrogen and negative carbanion.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What happens during the subsequent steps from $R-\text{NH}_2^+-\bar{\text{C}}\text{Cl}_2$ to form the isocyanide?

options.text: Addition of water to the carbene
Successive base-assisted deprotonations of nitrogen accompanied by loss of two chloride ions (two successive $\beta$-eliminations of $\text{HCl}$)

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Base abstracts the two protons from nitrogen while two chloride ions leave from carbon, generating the carbon-nitrogen triple bond.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: Can urea ($\text{H}_2\text{NCONH}_2$) give a positive carbylamine test?

options.text: No, because the amine nitrogens are in resonance with the carbonyl oxygen and are not nucleophilic enough
Yes, it gives two molecules of isocyanide
Yes, but only in boiling water

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Urea is a diamide; resonance delocalization of both amine lone pairs into the carbonyl group suppresses carbene attack completely.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What happens when an alkyl isocyanide is heated at elevated temperatures ($>200^\circ\text{C}$)?

options.text: It decomposes into alkene and ammonia
It rearranges to the thermodynamically more stable alkyl cyanide (nitrile): $R-\text{NC} \xrightarrow{\Delta} R-\text{CN}$
It explodes into carbon and nitrogen gas

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: The isonitrile-nitrile rearrangement is an exothermic unimolecular isomerization that converts the less stable isocyanide into the more stable nitrile ($R-\text{CN}$).

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the state of matter of phenyl isocyanide at room temperature?

options.text: A pale yellow liquid with a repulsive, sickening odor

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Phenyl isocyanide is a volatile, foul-smelling liquid (boiling point $\approx 166^\circ\text{C}$).

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What test can differentiate between aniline and $N$-methylaniline?

options.text: Carbylamine test (aniline gives a positive test with intolerable smell; $N$-methylaniline is negative)

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Aniline ($1^\circ$) reacts with $\text{CHCl}_3/\text{KOH}$ to give foul phenyl isocyanide; $N$-methylaniline ($2^\circ$) shows no reaction.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What test can differentiate between ethylamine and triethylamine?

options.text: Carbylamine test (positive for ethylamine, negative for triethylamine)

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Ethylamine is a primary amine and gives the carbylamine reaction; triethylamine is a tertiary amine and does not react.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: In the preparation of isocyanides by Carbylamine reaction, why is the yield typically moderate ($40-60\%$)?

options.text: Because isocyanides evaporate into space immediately
Due to side reactions of dichlorocarbene with solvent/water and formation of formamide byproducts
Because chloroform is converted to diamond
Because potassium chloride prevents product formation

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Dichlorocarbene can be hydrolyzed by hydroxide to carbon monoxide and formate, and some amine undergoes formylation, lowering isolated yields.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the oxidation number of carbon in the $-\text{NC}$ group compared to the $-\text{CN}$ group?

options.text: Carbon is in the $+2$ oxidation state in $-\text{NC}$, whereas it is in the $+4$ (or $+2$ relative to alkyl) oxidation state in $-\text{CN}$
Carbon has identical oxidation states in both

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: In $R-\text{N}\equiv\text{C}$, the terminal carbon has a lone pair and is bonded only to more electronegative nitrogen, giving it a $+2$ formal oxidation state (acting as divalent carbon).

Carbylamine Reaction.question: Can cyclohexylamine undergo the carbylamine reaction?

options.text: No, because the cyclohexane ring undergoes cleavage
No, it undergoes aromatization to benzene
Yes, it is a primary aliphatic amine and produces cyclohexyl isocyanide with a foul odor

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Cyclohexylamine possesses a primary $-\text{NH}_2$ group and undergoes normal carbylamine reaction to yield cyclohexyl isocyanide.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: Why is aqueous $\text{HCl}$ used to clean glassware after performing the carbylamine test?

options.text: It rapidly destroys traces of volatile, toxic isocyanides by hydrolyzing them into harmless ammonium salts and formic acid
It makes the glass shine brighter

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Isocyanides are toxic and possess lingering unbearable odors; washing equipment with dilute $\text{HCl}$ instantly destroys them by acidic hydrolysis.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: Which of the following undergoes $\alpha$-elimination fastest with base?
Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: The three electronegative chlorines in chloroform stabilize the conjugate trichloromethyl carbanion inductively, making chloroform's CH proton far more acidic ($pK_a \approx 15$) than those in $\text{CH}_2\text{Cl}_2$ or $\text{CH}_3\text{Cl}$.

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the organic product of the reaction: $\text{CH}_3\text{NH}_2 + \text{CHCl}_3 + 3\text{KOH} \xrightarrow{\Delta} P \xrightarrow{4[\text{H}], \text{LiAlH}_4} Q$?
Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Methylamine gives methyl isocyanide ($P$), which upon reduction with $\text{LiAlH}_4$ yields the secondary amine dimethylamine ($Q$).

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What happens when an isocyanide is treated with ozone ($\text{O}_3$)?

options.text: It is cleaved to an aldehyde and $\text{NO}_2$
It is oxidized to an alkyl isocyanate ($R-\text{N=C=O}$)

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: Ozone oxidizes the divalent terminal carbon of the isocyanide to form an isocyanate ($R-\text{N=C=O}$).

Carbylamine Reaction.question: What is the definitive conclusion when an unknown amine gives a vile, foul-smelling liquid upon warming with $\text{CHCl}_3$ and alcoholic $\text{KOH}$?

options.text: The unknown amine is confirmed to be a primary ($1^\circ$) amine
The unknown amine is a secondary ($2^\circ$) amine
The unknown amine is a tertiary ($3^\circ$) amine
The unknown amine is a quaternary salt

Carbylamine Reaction.explanation: The carbylamine test is uniquely selective for primary amines; only primary amines generate volatile, foul-smelling isocyanides under these conditions.

Haloform Reaction.question: Which of the following reagent combinations is employed in the standard Iodoform test?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: The haloform/iodoform reaction uses iodine in the presence of sodium hydroxide (generating sodium hypoiodite, $\text{NaOI}$, in situ).

Haloform Reaction.question: What structural feature is mandatory for a compound to give a positive Iodoform test?

options.text: A primary alcohol with at least four carbons
A $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}=\text{O}$ (methyl carbonyl) or $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(OH)}-$ (secondary methyl carbinol) group
A carboxylic acid group attached to an aromatic ring

Haloform Reaction.explanation: Only compounds containing a methyl ketone ($-\text{COCH}_3$) or a methyl carbinol group ($-\text{CH(OH)CH}_3$) oxidizable to a methyl ketone give positive iodoform tests.

Haloform Reaction.question: Which of the following primary alcohols gives a positive Iodoform test?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Ethanol is the ONLY primary alcohol that yields a positive iodoform test, because it is oxidized in situ to acetaldehyde ($\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}$).

Haloform Reaction.question: Which of the following aldehydes gives a positive Iodoform test?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Acetaldehyde is the ONLY aldehyde that contains the $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}=\text{O}$ group and gives a positive iodoform test.

Haloform Reaction.question: What is the physical appearance and characteristic of the precipitate formed in the Iodoform test?

options.text: Bright yellow crystalline precipitate with a characteristic medicinal/antiseptic odor (m.p. $119^\circ\text{C}$)

Haloform Reaction.explanation: Iodoform ($\text{CHI}_3$) forms bright yellow crystals with a distinct antiseptic odor and melts at $119^\circ\text{C}$.

Haloform Reaction.question: What are the organic products formed when propan-2-one (acetone) is treated with $\text{I}_2$ and $\text{NaOH}$?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_3 + 3\text{I}_2 + 4\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CHI}_3\downarrow + \text{CH}_3\text{COONa} + 3\text{NaI} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Haloform Reaction.question: How many moles of $\text{I}_2$ and $\text{NaOH}$ are consumed per mole of a methyl ketone (e.g., acetone) in the haloform reaction?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Tri-iodination of the $\alpha$-methyl consumes $3\text{I}_2 + 3\text{NaOH}$, and cleavage of the tri-iodoketone consumes 1 additional mole of $\text{NaOH}$, totaling $3\text{I}_2$ and $4\text{NaOH}$.

Haloform Reaction.question: How many moles of $\text{I}_2$ and $\text{NaOH}$ are consumed per mole of ethanol in the iodoform reaction?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: One mole of $\text{I}_2$ and 2 moles of $\text{NaOH}$ are consumed to oxidize ethanol to acetaldehyde, plus $3\text{I}_2 + 4\text{NaOH}$ for haloform conversion, totaling $4\text{I}_2$ and $6\text{NaOH}$.

Haloform Reaction.question: Which of the following pairs of compounds can be chemically distinguished using the Iodoform test?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Pentan-2-one has a methyl ketone group and gives a positive iodoform test (yellow ppt), whereas pentan-3-one does not.

Haloform Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds will NOT give a yellow precipitate of iodoform on treatment with $\text{I}_2/\text{NaOH}$?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Benzophenone has two phenyl rings attached to the carbonyl group and no methyl group, so it cannot undergo the haloform reaction.

Haloform Reaction.question: What is the leaving group in the final cleavage step of the haloform reaction of a methyl ketone?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Hydroxide attacks the carbonyl carbon of the trihalomethyl ketone; the stable trihalomethyl carbanion ($:\text{CX}_3^-$) is expelled as leaving group, followed by rapid proton transfer.

Haloform Reaction.question: Why does the halogenation of the $\alpha$-methyl group in base occur progressively faster with each halogen atom introduced?

options.text: Halogen atoms sterically repel the base, accelerating collision
Halogens increase the basicity of the carbonyl oxygen
Halogens convert the ketone into an alkene
Each electronegative halogen atom increases the acidity of the remaining $\alpha$-protons by strong $-I$ inductive effect

Haloform Reaction.explanation: The strongly electron-withdrawing halogens stabilize the conjugate base (enolate) through inductive electron withdrawal, making each successive $\alpha$-proton more acidic.

Haloform Reaction.question: When acetophenone is treated with $\text{I}_2$ and aqueous $\text{NaOH}$, what is the sodium carboxylate salt formed?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: $\text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COCH}_3 + 3\text{I}_2 + 4\text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CHI}_3\downarrow + \text{C}_6\text{H}_5\text{COONa} + 3\text{NaI} + 3\text{H}_2\text{O}$. The salt is sodium benzoate.

Haloform Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds gives a positive haloform test AND also forms an oxime with hydroxylamine?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Butan-2-one is a carbonyl compound (methyl ketone), so it reacts with hydroxylamine to form an oxime and gives a positive haloform test.

Haloform Reaction.question: Why does acetic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$) NOT give an iodoform test despite containing a methyl group adjacent to a carbonyl?

options.text: It has a boiling point that is too low
Base rapidly deprotonates the carboxylic acid to a carboxylate anion ($\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$), whose resonance suppresses further enolate formation and nucleophilic attack

Haloform Reaction.explanation: Deprotonation of $-\text{COOH}$ gives $-\text{COO}^-$. The negative charge strongly destabilizes any enolate formation on the adjacent methyl group.

Haloform Reaction.question: Does ethyl acetoacetate ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{COOCH}_2\text{CH}_3$) give a positive iodoform test?

options.text: No, because it is an ester
No, because the active methylene group prevents any halogenation
No, it only gives the biuret test
Yes, the methyl ketone group undergoes haloform cleavage under alkaline iodine conditions

Haloform Reaction.explanation: Ethyl acetoacetate has a terminal $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}=\text{O}$ unit which undergoes tri-iodination and haloform cleavage to yield iodoform.

Haloform Reaction.question: Which of the following dicarbonyl compounds gives iodoform when treated with $\text{I}_2/\text{NaOH}$?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Acetylacetone has two methyl ketone groups; cleavage of both yields iodoform and acetate/carbonate.

Haloform Reaction.question: Which haloform is a volatile liquid with a characteristic sweet chloroform smell, used historically as an anesthetic?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Chloroform is a colorless volatile liquid ($b.p. \approx 61^\circ\text{C}$) with a sweetish smell, prepared by the haloform reaction using $\text{Cl}_2$ or bleaching powder.

Haloform Reaction.question: What reagent can be used in place of $\text{Cl}_2 + \text{NaOH}$ for industrial preparation of chloroform from ethanol or acetone?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Bleaching powder acting as both an oxidizing agent and a chlorinating agent in water supplies $\text{Ca(OCl)}_2$ and $\text{Ca(OH)}_2$ for haloform reaction.

Haloform Reaction.question: When but-3-en-2-one ($\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCOCH}_3$) undergoes haloform reaction with $\text{I}_2/\text{NaOH}$ followed by acidification, the product containing the double bond is:
Haloform Reaction.explanation: The haloform reaction selectively cleaves the methyl ketone to a carboxylate while leaving isolated or conjugated double bonds intact; acidification yields acrylic acid.

Haloform Reaction.question: Which of the following isomeric alcohols of molecular formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ gives a positive Iodoform test?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Butan-2-ol has the $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)}-$ motif and is oxidized by hypoiodite to butan-2-one, which gives yellow iodoform ppt.

Haloform Reaction.question: Why does 2-methylpropan-2-ol ($\text{tert}$-butanol) fail to give an Iodoform test?

options.text: It does not contain any carbon atoms
It is a tertiary alcohol and cannot be oxidized to a methyl carbonyl compound by hypoiodite
It contains no hydrogen atoms on the methyl groups

Haloform Reaction.explanation: Tertiary alcohols lack an $\alpha$-hydrogen on the carbinol carbon and cannot undergo the initial oxidation step to a ketone.

Haloform Reaction.question: In the haloform reaction of acetone with bromine and base (Bromoform reaction), what is the formula of the product formed?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Reaction of acetone with $\text{Br}_2/\text{NaOH}$ produces bromoform (tribromomethane, $\text{CHBr}_3$).

Haloform Reaction.question: What test can be used to distinguish between benzaldehyde and acetophenone?

options.text: Tollens\' test (acetophenone gives silver mirror, benzaldehyde does not)
Fehling\'s test (acetophenone reduces Fehling\'s, benzaldehyde does not)
Iodoform test (acetophenone gives yellow ppt of $\text{CHI}_3$, benzaldehyde does not)

Haloform Reaction.explanation: Acetophenone is a methyl ketone and gives positive iodoform test; benzaldehyde lacks a methyl group and gives negative test.

Haloform Reaction.question: What happens when iodoform ($\text{CHI}_3$) is heated with silver powder (Ag)?

options.text: Silver iodide dissolves completely to form silver metal

Haloform Reaction.explanation: $2\text{CHI}_3 + 6\text{Ag} \xrightarrow{\Delta} \text{CH}\equiv\text{CH} + 6\text{AgI}\downarrow$. This is a classic dehalogenation coupling reaction.

Haloform Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds yields a yellow precipitate with $\text{I}_2/\text{NaOH}$ AND also reduces Tollens\' reagent?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Acetaldehyde is an aldehyde (reduces Tollens\' reagent to silver mirror) AND contains a $\text{CH}_3-\text{C}=\text{O}$ group (gives positive iodoform test).

Haloform Reaction.question: What is the role of sodium hydroxide in the first step of the haloform reaction?

options.text: Nucleophilic attack on the halogen molecule
Deprotonation of the $\alpha$-methyl carbon to form an enolate ion

Haloform Reaction.explanation: Hydroxide deprotonates the $\alpha$-carbon, forming an enolate carbanion that subsequently attacks iodine.

Haloform Reaction.question: Which of the following secondary alcohols does NOT give the iodoform test?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Pentan-3-ol oxidizes to pentan-3-one, which has ethyl groups on both sides and no methyl carbonyl group, so it gives negative test.

Haloform Reaction.question: What is the oxidation state of carbon in iodoform ($\text{CHI}_3$)?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: In $\text{CHI}_3$, $\text{H}$ is +1 and each $\text{I}$ is -1. Thus $x + 1 + 3(-1) = 0 \implies x = +2$.

Haloform Reaction.question: An unknown liquid gives a positive 2,4-DNP test, a negative Fehling\'s test, and a positive iodoform test. The liquid is:
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Positive 2,4-DNP indicates carbonyl; negative Fehling\'s indicates ketone or aromatic aldehyde; positive iodoform indicates methyl ketone (acetophenone).

Haloform Reaction.question: Why does lactic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)COOH}$) give a positive iodoform test?

options.text: It contains the secondary methyl carbinol group $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(OH)}-$
It has a ketone group already present

Haloform Reaction.explanation: Lactic acid contains $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(OH)}-$, which is oxidized by hypoiodite to pyruvic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCOOH}$), which then undergoes haloform cleavage.

Haloform Reaction.question: Which halogen gives a yellow solid product that is easily identifiable by visual inspection in the haloform reaction?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Iodoform is an insoluble yellow crystalline solid, making iodine the preferred halogen for qualitative analytical detection.

Haloform Reaction.question: Reaction of 1-phenylethan-1-ol with $\text{I}_2$ and $\text{NaOH}$ yields:
Haloform Reaction.explanation: 1-Phenylethanol is oxidized to acetophenone, which undergoes haloform cleavage to give yellow $\text{CHI}_3$ and sodium benzoate.

Haloform Reaction.question: What is the primary reason why tertiary alcohols NEVER give a haloform test?

options.text: They are too acidic to react with base
They lack an $\alpha$-hydrogen and cannot be oxidized to a carbonyl intermediate under the alkaline hypoiodite reaction conditions
They decompose instantly into alkenes at room temperature
They react with iodine to form insoluble complexes

Haloform Reaction.explanation: Hypoiodite is a mild oxidant that oxidizes $2^\circ$ methyl carbinols via $\alpha$-H abstraction; $3^\circ$ alcohols lack an $\alpha$-hydrogen.

Haloform Reaction.question: What is formed when chloral hydrate is treated with aqueous $\text{NaOH}$?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Chloral hydrate undergoes haloform cleavage: $\text{CCl}_3\text{CH(OH)}_2 + \text{NaOH} \rightarrow \text{CHCl}_3 + \text{HCOONa} + \text{H}_2\text{O}$.

Haloform Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds gives a positive iodoform test?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Butan-2-ol contains the $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(OH)}-$ group, oxidizable to butan-2-one which gives positive iodoform test.

Haloform Reaction.question: What is the theoretical yield of iodoform from 0.1 mole of acetone reacting with excess $\text{I}_2/\text{NaOH}$?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: One mole of acetone produces one mole of iodoform ($1:1$ molar stoichiometry); hence 0.1 mole acetone gives 0.1 mole $\text{CHI}_3$.

Haloform Reaction.question: In the haloform reaction of butan-2-one with $\text{I}_2/\text{NaOH}$, the carboxylate product formed is:
Haloform Reaction.explanation: The methyl carbon is cleaved as $\text{CHI}_3$, leaving the three-carbon fragment as propanoate: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_3 \rightarrow \text{CHI}_3 + \text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COONa}$.

Haloform Reaction.question: Why is the haloform reaction useful synthetically for converting methyl ketones to carboxylic acids?

options.text: It increases the carbon chain length by one carbon
It selectively reduces carbonyl groups to alcohols
It oxidizes methyl ketones to carboxylic acids with one less carbon atom without affecting non-conjugated $\text{C}=\text{C}$ double bonds elsewhere in the molecule
It converts carboxylic acids into methyl ketones

Haloform Reaction.explanation: Haloform oxidation provides a mild, selective method to convert $R-\text{COCH}_3$ into $R-\text{COOH}$ (one less carbon), tolerating double bonds.

Haloform Reaction.question: Which of the following compounds will give positive iodoform test?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Pyruvic acid has a $\text{CH}_3\text{CO}-$ group attached to $-\text{COOH}$ and gives yellow iodoform precipitate upon treatment with $\text{I}_2/\text{NaOH}$.

Haloform Reaction.question: Which of the following pairs of isomers can be distinguished by the iodoform test?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: 1-Phenylethanol has a methyl carbinol group $\text{CH}_3-\text{CH(OH)}-$ and gives positive iodoform test; 2-phenylethanol is a primary alcohol and does not.

Haloform Reaction.question: What happens when chloroform is stored in clear glass bottles in the presence of air and sunlight?

options.text: It decomposes into carbon tetrachloride and water
It slowly oxidizes to produce poisonous phosgene gas ($\text{COCl}_2$)

Haloform Reaction.explanation: $2\text{CHCl}_3 + \text{O}_2 \xrightarrow{h\nu} 2\text{COCl}_2 + 2\text{HCl}$. Phosgene (carbonyl chloride) is highly toxic; hence chloroform is stored in dark amber bottles with 1% ethanol as stabilizer.

Haloform Reaction.question: Why is 1% ethanol added to commercial chloroform bottles?

options.text: It prevents the evaporation of chloroform
It increases the anesthetic potency of chloroform
It reacts with any phosgene formed to convert it into harmless diethyl carbonate
It serves as a dye to detect impurities

Haloform Reaction.explanation: Ethanol acts as a chemical scavenger: $\text{COCl}_2 + 2\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH} \rightarrow (\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{O})_2\text{CO} + 2\text{HCl}$, converting phosgene into non-toxic diethyl carbonate.

Haloform Reaction.question: Which of the following gives iodoform test?
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Acetylacetone (pentane-2,4-dione) contains two methyl ketone groups and gives a vigorous positive iodoform test.

Haloform Reaction.question: An organic compound $A$ on treatment with $\text{I}_2/\text{NaOH}$ gives yellow precipitate of iodoform. On mild oxidation with $\text{Cu}$ at $300^\circ\text{C}$, it gives compound $B$ which also gives positive iodoform test. Compound $A$ is:
Haloform Reaction.explanation: Propan-2-ol ($A$) gives positive iodoform test. On dehydrogenation over $\text{Cu}$ at $300^\circ\text{C}$ it yields acetone ($B$), which also gives positive iodoform test.
